en: The Subāhuparipṛcchā Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of India during the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Command.
Chapter One: The Classification of Discipline (Vinayavibhanga). Chapter One: The Classification of Discipline.
At that time, the Vajradhara Bodhisattva, Great Yakṣa General, whose power was inconceivable and whose radiance surpassed a thousand suns, dwelt with single-minded concentration.
Within that great assembly, there was a youth named Subāhu, whose great compassion was profound and sincere.
Immediately rising from his seat, he prostrated with devotion at the feet of Vajrapāṇi, then bowed with palms joined and said:
"O Greatly Powerful Honored One, I have harbored doubts for a long time and wish to ask a few questions; I pray only that you will grant me your permission."
At that time, the Great Yakṣa General Vajrapāṇi said:
"Regarding what you doubt, ask whatever you wish; I shall resolve your doubts for you and eliminate them."
The youth Subāhu said: "I now request the permission of your venerable majesty to ask whatever I wish.

I have long harbored a doubt: observing all those among the renunciants and householders, both men and women, throughout the world who, seeking to escape the ocean of birth and death, search for the dhāraṇī methods for swift accomplishment, restricting their food, reciting with single-minded diligence and hardship—yet despite such practice, they still do not achieve success."
I only pray that the Venerable One will analyze and explain the causes and conditions for non-attainment as well as the methods for attainment.
Your venerable majesty and compassionate light can eliminate the source of the most grievous suffering of sentient beings;
the mantras you proclaim can further destroy all obstacles.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the causes, practicing the six perfections to the ultimate degree of equality and subtlety; his practices and vows are not in vain.
All the teachings he bestows are for the sake of sentient beings, leading them forward toward Bodhi.

For what reason do sentient beings who recite mantras fail to obtain their fruits? They seek the mantras from their teachers, encompassing all dharmas—superior, middling, and inferior—and practice them from day to month, from month to year, and from year until the end of their lives, performing ascetic disciplines without ceasing day or night, yet they still receive no efficacious results.
If that which is performed according to the ritual fails to achieve its result, then these mantra syllables cannot be relied upon;
yet if they must be relied upon, there has never been a single instance of their efficacy being proven through practice.
The World-Honored One has established this teaching: if one can maintain and recite the mantra, one will immediately attain wisdom and be freed from ignorance;
because ignorance is severed, there is quiescent liberation.
If this were so, why would one not obtain the fruit of siddhi as desired?
One should abandon mantras and instead follow ignorance; what need is there to laboriously recite mantras in pursuit of siddhi?

The teachings of all noble ones are never given in vain. When sentient beings give rise to a mind, stir a thought, or form an intention to seek [the Dharma], the Bodhisattva—possessing the knowledge of others' minds—fulfills their vows and bestows the supreme bliss. For what reason, then, do the wishes of seeking sentient beings remain unfulfilled, why do those in suffering fail to obtain the fruit of happiness, and why are immeasurable sentient beings caused to fall into doubt and slander?

I have heard that all noble ones never speak falsely; when sentient beings hear their teachings and practice according to the Dharma, they immediately perceive the right path and obtain boundless rewards.
How is it that karma produces its fruit?
Is it because the conditions are incomplete,
or is it because the proper season has not arrived?
Is it because you cannot obtain the sun?
Is it because you cannot obtain the moon?
Or is it because you cannot obtain the stars?
Is it because a suitable location has not been found?
Is it because the location is impure?
Or is it because the offerings are incomplete?
Is it because you have failed to find companions?
Is it because you lack single-minded devotion?
Or is it because of negligence?
Is it due to excessive sitting?
Is it due to mental dullness?
Or is it due to excessive discursive thought?
Is it that your body is impure?
Is it that your robes are impure?
Or is it that the lamp you have lit is not [proper]?
Is it that the food vessels are not in accordance with the Dharma?
Is it that the flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma?
Or is it that the food is placed [upon them] in an improper manner?
Is it that the ghee, curd, and milk are not prepared according to the Dharma?
Or is it that the invitation of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and other spirits is not performed according to the Dharma?
Does it mean that the practitioner has consumed food that was touched by others?
Or that the practitioner has passed through a defiled place?
Or that the practitioner has sat or slept on the same bed as a woman?
"Has the practitioner of recitation consumed the five pungent roots?
Has the practitioner of recitation stolen property belonging to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha?
Has the practitioner of recitation plundered all sentient beings and deceived the orphaned and the destitute?"
Is it that you do not practice the six perfections?
Is it that you do not make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha?
Is it that you do not make offerings to all spiritual friends and all sentient beings?
Is it because you have treated all sentient beings with contempt?
Is it because you have invoked the homa in an improper manner?
Or is it because there were additions or omissions in the words and phrases of the mantra?
Is it because the medicinal flavors are not fully prepared?
Is it because the vessels do not conform to the Dharma?
Or is it because the scented water was poured below in an improper manner?
Is it that you do not bathe the honored images?
Is it that you do not practice walking meditation?
Is it that you do not practice seated meditation?
Is it because you have not washed your hands and feet and are thus impure?
Is it because you have not chewed a tooth-stick?
Or is it because you have rinsed your mouth and remain impure?
Was it because the washing was not performed according to the Dharma?
Was it because the gathering of flowers was not performed according to the Dharma?
Or was it because the disciples were not acting according to the Dharma?
Is it because the master who serves as the preceptor for the disciples has a distracted mind?
Or is it because the disciples have not prepared the food according to the Dharma?
Or is it because the person performing the recitation has defiled the pure food with their hands?
When performing the homa, did you blow upon the fire with your mouth?
Was the fuel not prepared according to the Dharma?
Or did you offer leftover food as an offering to the Buddha?
Is it because the practitioner of recitation eats leftover food?
Is it because the practitioner does not recite the sutras during the two prescribed times?
Or is it because they have disobeyed their preceptors and teachers?
Is it because you have acted rebelliously toward your parents?
Is it because you have not received the instructions and commands of your teacher?
Or is it because those who recite the mantras speak too much of worldly affairs?
Is it for the sake of seeking fame and profit?
Is it for the sake of seeking renown?
Or is it for the sake of performing worldly activities with fervor?
Is it because the rites were not performed according to the rules during the waxing moon?
Is it because the rites were not performed according to the rules during the waning moon?
Or is it because the five planets have lost their proper courses and the rites were not performed?
Is it because no ritual was performed during an eclipse of the sun or moon?
Is it because the boundary (sīmā) was not properly established?
Or is it because the protection of the body was not properly performed?
Was it that your sitting and rising were not in accordance with the Dharma?
Was it that your coming and going were not in accordance with the Dharma?
Or was it that your eating was not in accordance with the Dharma?
When partaking of the formal meal, do you fail to visualize the honored deities of the five families?
Or do you fail to visualize the honored deity of your own particular family?

When performing the great offering, if you do not seal and protect all the food vessels, as well as the food and drink themselves, and they thus become improper, will Māra find an opportunity to exploit this?
Did you fail to perform the ritual for opening the door upon entering the vihāra?
Or was it when you wished to recite the mantras that you conversed with a eunuch?
Or did you converse with a maiden or a widow while staying together with them?
"Should one not sit regardless of the ground?
Regarding such matters of defilement and transgression, I am currently entirely unaware of them; how much less could future sentient beings comprehend such things?"

I only pray that the Venerable One will give rise to great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings, by instructing us in the ritual procedures and the dhāraṇī recitation methods, as well as performing the homa rites for the three kinds of siddhi, so that efficacy may be swiftly realized and future sentient beings may each follow this practice to all ascend to liberation.
At that time, when the Vajradhara Bodhisattva Mahāyakṣa General had heard these questions posed by the youth Subāhu, he spoke after a brief moment:
"Excellent, excellent!
Young man, you take pity upon all sentient beings, and your compassion pervades them all, like the moonlight that shines universally upon the world.
Because of this mind of yours, characterized by supreme great compassion, you have already surpassed the bodhicitta of all the great bodhisattvas.
This gateway of adornment seeks no personal pleasure, yet is able to endure great suffering for the benefit of sentient beings.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva sees the suffering of sentient beings, he himself suffers;
when he sees the happiness of sentient beings, he himself is happy.
I observe that your mind is ultimately not for your own sake, but has given rise to such a question for the benefit of sentient beings.
Now, with a single-minded focus, contemplate carefully and receive my teaching; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"If there are those who uphold and recite the methods of all mantras, they should first give rise to profound reverence for the Buddhas;

next, they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta, extensively making great vows to deliver sentient beings, and remain far removed from the karmas of greed, delusion, pride, and the like;
furthermore, they should develop deep veneration for the Triple Gem and also reverently honor the Great Vajra Family."
One must distance oneself from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and double-tongued speech; furthermore, one should neither drink alcohol nor eat meat.

Though one may recite mantras with the mouth, if the mind and intentions are not virtuous and one constantly practices wrong views, then by virtue of those wrong views, it becomes unwholesome and yields a defiled fruit.
It is like cultivating a field according to the seasons: if the seeds are scorched, they will never sprout.
Ignorance and false views are likewise thus: even if one performs wholesome deeds, one will ultimately not obtain their fruit.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from false views, constantly rely upon right view without wavering, and practice the ten wholesome paths to increase the profound and subtle Dharma.

If there are devas, nāgas, asuras, and other such beings, as well as various classes of malevolent spirits that feed on flesh and blood, who roam the world to harm sentient beings and disturb the minds of those practicing recitation, causing them distraction—upon seeing one correctly upholding this sublime mantra method, they will immediately give rise to terror, for this dharma is utterly opposed to them.

If one wishes to prevent those who recite mantras from retreating from bodhicitta and desires that they remain unharmed, they must enter this Great Samaya Maṇḍala; because it is the dwelling place of all the great noble assemblies and the various devas, it is therefore called the Great Maṇḍala.

Furthermore, one must enter the wondrous maṇḍala of the rites for performing various activities; moreover, in order to subdue all the celestial deities, the palaces of Māra, and so forth, one must again enter the supreme Great Maṇḍala of the Vidyārāja.

Furthermore, regarding the entry into the great maṇḍala of all mantras as previously described—the sublime samaya—it is for the purpose of enabling the practitioner to extinguish their transgressions; therefore, one must enter it repeatedly.

Furthermore, having entered the sublime maṇḍalas of the various messengers and others, as well as the immeasurable vidyārājñīs and queens, and thus having universally entered the maṇḍalas where the vidyās of the mass of merit dwell, all the māras, seeing that person from afar, will harbor great fear in their hearts and scatter in every direction.

Because one enters various maṇḍalas through recitation and is empowered by the assembly of noble ones, when the māras behold this practitioner of mantra-recitation, they will all flee in terror as if from the abode of a vajra-possessing lord in his full majesty, or like a mass of blazing fire; they shall be unable to cause harm, and the worldly and supramundane vidyā-mantras will swiftly attain accomplishment.

If one does not enter this great maṇḍala, lacks compassion and the bodhicitta, shows no reverence for the Buddhas, and takes refuge in other external deities while reciting the mantras of the Buddha-dharma, such a person will bring about their own ruin.

"If a practitioner of recitation is unable to enter all the maṇḍalas, they should, within them, perform at least one samaya; with a mind of deep reverence, they should prostrate to the master who bestows empowerment and request empowerment. Having received empowerment, they may perform any one activity according to their respective family, whereby they will be able to prevent all yakṣas, nāga kings, and various evil māras, vināyakas, and fierce deities from causing disturbance."

The practitioner must first maintain the precepts; just as all sprouts and seeds grow depending upon the earth, which they cause to flourish through diligent irrigation, so too should one practice the Dharma of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*) taught by the World-Honored One, fully endowed with pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one belongs to the secular class, with the sole exception of monastic robes, there is no difference whatsoever regarding the remaining vows of discipline (*vinaya*).
One must necessarily remain far removed from all defiled phenomena and fully practice the teachings expounded by the Sugata.
The ritual rules for mantras are likewise thus: if the practitioner becomes weary while reciting, they should read Mahāyāna sūtras.

Furthermore, those who wish to extinguish their transgressions should go to a secluded and pure place and, using either fragrant mud or exquisite sand, cast ten thousand *stūpas* as a seal—more is even better.

Internally, one should install the Verse on the Dharmakāya of Dependent Origination; or, before a reliquary stupa or a sacred image, one should use unguents, scatter flowers, burn incense, light lamps, hang banners, pennants, and canopies, and with sublime sounds, offer praise and worship to the Buddhas without interruption.
"First, one must have a good companion; if one can achieve accomplishment without a companion, such a thing is impossible.
It is like a carriage that lacks one of its wheels: even if the driver is skilled, it cannot move forward."
Reciting mantras without a companion is likewise so; even if one exerts oneself with diligent toil, in the end, nothing will be accomplished.
Furthermore, that companion must be endowed with wisdom, be pure, clean, and dignified, and born of a noble lineage;
they must be courageous and fearless, capable of disciplining the sense faculties, and possessing the power of joyful renunciation.
One who is able to endure the afflictions of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat without giving rise to regression:
delights in making offerings to preceptors and instructors, constantly cherishes their kindness and righteousness,
and maintains a profound mind of reverence toward the Triple Gem.

Such practitioners as these are extremely difficult to encounter; if one is accompanied by such companions—whether one, two, three, four, or five, or even more—the practitioner of mantras will certainly attain success and merit, and thus one must seek out such companions.
2. Chapter on the Classification of Locations, from the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Chapter Two: "Furthermore, Subāhu, the youth!"

If a practitioner of recitation seeks swift accomplishment, they should seek out places where various Buddhas have previously dwelt, or where Bodhisattvas have dwelt, or where Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas have dwelt; in such locations, devas, nāgas, and others constantly offer worship and provide protection.
Therefore, those who perform recitation should first purify their body and mind and be fully endowed with the precepts (*vinaya*). They should always reside in such superior locations.

If one does not encounter such a blessed site, one may also dwell by the side of a great river, or near a small stream, a pond, or a marsh; a place where famous flowers flourish and thrive is also suitable.
One should stay away from noisy crowds and not dwell among them.
The water should be clear and flowing, full and overflowing, free from aquatic creatures or venomous insects;
or one may dwell in a secluded and pure place among the mountains, where soft grass grows and flowers and fruits abound.
Alternatively, one may dwell on mountain slopes or within rock caves where there are no fearsome or venomous beasts.

In such locations, one should dig deeply to a depth of one *hasta* (cubit), thoroughly clearing away all thorns, potsherds, chaff, bones, hair, ashes, charcoal, saline soil, and the burrows of insects; if the digging is not sufficient even after reaching such depths, one should abandon that site and seek another location.

Having obtained it, one should cultivate and refine it according to the method previously described; the excavated site should be filled with pure earth, and a vihāra should be constructed upon that ground, ensuring it is extremely solid so that no violent winds may enter the room;
the wall crevices should be plastered so that fleas and ants have no place to dwell;
and the roof of the dwelling should be well-covered so that water does not leak in.
Windows should be installed on all four walls, ensuring they are extremely bright and clean.
A door should be placed in the room facing east, west, north, or south; however, a door must not be placed on the southern side.
Once the construction is complete, smear the interior of the chamber with cow dung.

In accordance with the methods appropriate for that specific ritual, install the sacred image; whether the image is painted in colors or carved, it may be made of copper, gold, or silver—whichever one can afford—and all such offerings are acceptable.

The material for the painting should be fine, soft, and densely woven white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), produced by skilled artisans. Both ends must remain with their threads intact and not be cut; it should be of wide width, free of loose fibers, and never previously used. First, it must be thoroughly washed and then sprinkled with scented water. The pigments used for the painting should not be mixed with glue; they should be placed in a new vessel, and a brush made of cow hair should be used.
The person who paints the image should bathe until pure and observe the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), receiving them in this manner every day.

Once the image has been painted according to the ritual rules, one should place unguents, incense, flower garlands, food and drink, and lamps before it. After performing extensive offerings—including praise and prostration—one should then carry out the ritual procedure.
"What you seek shall be swiftly obtained, and your wishes will be fulfilled.
Furthermore, Su-ba-hu, youth!
If the practitioner is a layperson, they should likewise shave their head, leaving only the crown hair."
The robes one wears must all be red in color; alternatively, one may wear white garments, grass garments, bark garments, or cloth made of *kusha* grass.
One must carry four types of alms bowls:
those made of wood, iron, clay, or gourd. These bowls must be perfectly round, fine and dense, without cracks or defects, and free from leaks.
One should carry this vessel and go from house to house in due order to beg for food. Once one has obtained sufficient food, one should go near a clear spring and wash it clean with water.
When one wishes to eat the rice, one should first take the rice from the bowl and divide it into five portions:
one portion is intended for hungry people who may come along the road.
One portion is given to the sentient beings in the water;
one portion is given to the sentient beings on land;
and one portion is given to the parents of seven generations as well as the sentient beings who are hungry ghosts.
The fifth division concerns sufficiency and insufficiency regarding one's own food.

When about to eat, one should contemplate the rice in this bowl through the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) before consuming it; one should merely treat hunger as a disease and not crave delicious flavors.
When the meal was finished, he immediately went to a river, pond, or spring to bathe and rinse his mouth, cleaning his teeth with willow wood.

Emerging from the water and putting on his robes, he entered his meditation chamber; after performing three prostrations before the Buddha and making his vows, he left the pure chamber and performed walking meditation (caṅkrama) thirty to fifty times, after which he recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The place where one dwells should not be far from a village or town, yet it should not be too close to a populous area; it should be free of non-Buddhists and abundant in food and drink, and be a place where people constantly delight in giving and take refuge with faith in the Triple Gem—such a place should be chosen for the rains retreat.

Do not dwell with those of external paths or those who harbor pride; do not associate with those who rely on their noble lineage, who plunder the benefits of the Sangha among the ignorant, who lack compassion and mercy, who preach goodness with their mouths while harboring venomous snakes in their hearts, or who, relying upon the Buddha and the Sangha, seek only fame and profit. Be careful not to draw near such people; deeply respect and distance yourselves from this class of sentient beings.

Or when they see those who recite mantras and revere the teachings of the Śākya, such beings harbor poison in their hearts, reviling them with anger and abuse; claiming to have attained what they have not attained and to have realized what they have not realized, they seek out the faults of others, constantly watching for opportunities to cause disturbance and confusion, hoping that they may not find companionship.
"Excellent indeed! You are able to distinguish between good and evil.

We may meet from time to time so that you may employ skillful means to transform those people, causing the sprouts of the Way to grow. Do not yet speak of the profound and wondrous meaning when we first meet; because their roots of goodness are not yet mature, for now speak only of shallow and proximate meanings, so that they may gradually practice until they are finally able to enter the Great [Vehicle]."
"If the practitioner is of the Brahmin caste, they raise this objection:
'You are of the Brahmin caste; why do you recite the mantras of the Śākya teachings?'"

"You should study this for yourself and teach it to others; receive it yourself and bestow it upon others; perform sacrifices to the gods yourself and officiate as a priest for others. These six dharmas constitute your fundamental doctrine."
Furthermore, you must serve the sacrificial fire and act as this king; you must also take a wife and father a son to continue the lineage. Only by practicing these rites can you attain liberation.
Why then do you recite the mantras of the Śākya teachings?
"If the practitioner belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, they will raise this objection:
'You are of the noble Kṣatriya lineage; you ought to perform sacrifices, practice charity, and pursue self-study—these three things are the fundamental tenets of your own tradition.'"
"Furthermore, you must succeed in subduing and defeating your enemies; only by practicing this rite shall you attain liberation.
You should not study such mantras.
If the practitioner belongs to the Vaiśya caste, they raise this objection:

"You belong to the Vaiśya caste and are of lowly origin due to your mixed karma; you engage in trade for profit, greedily coveting the wealth of others, valuing the cheap while seeking the high-priced, manipulating measures and scales, and making false speech your profession—these are your ancestral occupations. How, then, can you hope to attain the recitation of mantras?"
"You should not study the mantras of the Śākya teachings.
If the practitioner belongs to the Śūdra caste, he will raise this objection:
"You are of the lowest Śūdra caste; you should engage in agriculture and should always provide offerings to pure-practicing Brahmins."

In this way, those various difficulties and afflictions that disturb the practitioner and seek to cause them to retreat—those evil people who are non-Buddhists not only harm others, but also bring harm upon themselves.

The dharma of the non-Buddhists involves eating after the noon hour; those who practice the Noble Path differ from them in this regard, and for that reason, one should not go to the dwellings of non-Buddhists to seek alms.
If there is a household where the five pungent roots, alcohol, or meat are kept, a practitioner of mantras must not eat therein even if they were to suffer from hunger for an entire kalpa.
Why is this? Because there is no difference between living with them and dwelling with a caṇḍāla.
One should not even go to their door to converse with such people, let alone eat with them.
If one eats that food, how is one any different from those people? It is not called pure conduct; one is likewise equal to a *caṇḍāla*.
One must distinguish this well, and while walking, sitting, standing, or staying still, one must apply the mind with careful observation before proceeding to come or go.

"As for the Dharma of the causes and effects of good and evil, there is no distinction between those with wisdom and those without, nor between Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; it is solely due to the false discriminations of the world that these provisional names are established."
If one can cultivate goodness, one shall realize nirvana.
If one does not speak of cause and effect, do not discuss the four castes; for all who commit evil deeds enter the evil realms to undergo suffering, not merely those of the four castes.
"Furthermore, Su-ba-hu youth!
Since beginningless time, the defiled bodies of sentient beings do not become pure through the purity of food, but rather through the purity of body and mind."
Only by severing unwholesome karma and cultivating all wholesome dharmas can one attain purity of body and mind.
It is like a person afflicted with sores and scabs who, thinking only of recovery, applies medicine to them.
The practitioner’s eating is also like this: they merely eliminate hunger and thirst, taking no pleasure in rich flavors.
Furthermore, there is a parable:
suppose there were a father and son who entered a vast desert; the road was long and arduous, and they were driven by hunger and thirst, until the man was compelled to eat his son’s flesh.
The practitioner’s eating is likewise thus: merely to eliminate the disease of hunger and not to become attached to its flavor.

When observing the donor who brings the food, one should feel fear and shame, thinking that the gift is difficult to digest; one should eat this meal with the thought that it is like eating the flesh of one's own child.
It is like weighing objects: as the weight shifts, one end of the scale sinks; if the object is light or small, that end immediately rises;
if the objects are equal in weight, the scale remains level.
The practitioner of recitation is likewise thus: one must not exceed the proper measure, nor should it be too few.
It is like an old house on the verge of collapsing; to prevent its ruin, one supports it with pillars.

The practitioner’s eating is also like this: it is solely for the sake of preserving the body in order to seek the ultimate fruit; one does not crave the flavors of food for the sake of desiring the body to remain long in the world.
For example, just as one must apply oil to a moving carriage, so too, for the sake of increasing wholesome qualities, should one partake of food.
Therefore, the Blessed One taught this Dharma: sentient beings in the desire realm subsist by means of nutriment.

The practitioner must constantly observe that his own body is like a plantain tree; he should not crave the flavors of the food and drink he consumes, and among the four types of alms bowls, he should take whichever one is appropriate, observing the sequence of begging for food during the four periods of the day.
The World-Honored One has taught that through wisdom and skillful means, one must subdue the six sense faculties so as not to become negligent.

Women use their physical beauty, clever smiles, and coquettish speech; by nature they delight in finery, their gait is seductive, and their gestures move the hearts of men, leading them into delusion and confusion.

A mantra-practitioner would rather have a spark of fire enter their eyes, causing them to lose both sight and become blind, than with a distracted mind gaze upon the forms of women, discriminating among their various marks, features, and exquisite beauty, which causes the practitioner’s recitation to lose its power.

Beg for alms according to circumstances without giving rise to attachment; tame the mind through right reflection; enter the homes of others with the conduct of a Muni, making no distinction between those of high, middle, or low status, or the poor and the humble.

Furthermore, one should not enter the home of a woman who has recently given birth; one should not go to where cattle, horses, donkeys, camels, pigs, dogs, or sheep have calved; nor should one go to places where many people drink alcohol, or to places where lewd men and women consort together in heedless indulgence.
One should not look upon places where many children play,
nor upon the wedding ceremonies of lay families;
nor upon houses with vicious dogs, nor upon places where performers provide musical entertainment.

If one has long been acquainted with a circle of companions who falsely claim, "I possess the mantras and verses; though I have never received transmission from a master, I forcefully profess that I understand the secret treasury of mantras and the principles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*," and among those without wisdom, they say, "I have heard and understood these things; I am fit to be your teacher," yet when questioned by a person of wisdom, they are like a mute sheep;
deceiving honest people of sincere heart while receiving wealth and property to support their wives and children;

with the three poisons of affliction—delusion, anger, and greed—within their hearts, and with pride as high as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), lacking even a single fraction of the resolve for enlightenment.

Those who falsely claim to understand the Buddha-dharma, showing arrogance toward the Triple Gem and deceiving all classes of people—whether elders, juniors, men, or women—commit boundless transgressions.
To speak briefly, one must not go to the aforementioned places to beg for alms; other locations may be visited as one pleases.

Having obtained food, one shall immediately return to one’s original place, wash one’s feet with water, and strictly follow the previously mentioned method of dividing the food: offer one portion to the Honored One, share one portion freely, and eat one portion oneself. As for the remainder, it is for the seven generations of ancestors—both terrestrial and aquatic—and for hungry ghosts; these have already been explained previously, so their names will not be listed again here.
"Eat only at the proper time and do not violate the rule against eating past midday.

Bathe three times a day, observing the correct timing and seasonal rhythms; offer flowers and apply fragrant unguents as an act of worship. Rub your hands with scented clay rather than engaging in verbal praise."

Do not omit the three sessions; ensure that the articles of offering are not defiled or contaminated. During the three sessions at night, offer only incense; rub your hands with scented clay, and do not form hand-mudrās with hands that have been touched [to impure objects].
When performing recitation, one should sit upon *kuśa* grass; if one cannot provide various miscellaneous offerings, even offering flowers and water is sufficient.
Regarding flowers and incense: all kinds of aquatic flowers, as well as various wild flowers from marshes and mountains, may all serve as offerings.
It is permitted to perform recitation while walking, standing, sitting, or pacing; however, one must not maintain recitation while lying down.
Once the recitation is completed, one should constantly contemplate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), observing their various merits so as not to allow the mind to become distracted.
Chapter Three: The Section on Removing Obstacles from the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*. "Furthermore, Subāhu, the Youth!..."

If a practitioner of recitation gives rise to even a single thought of any affliction such as greed, hatred, or delusion that merges with the mind, it is called the affliction of birth and death; if one eliminates this mind, one immediately attains purity.
The Buddhas always praise this Dharma, calling it liberation.
It is like pure water that is inherently free from defilement; it is only because of dust and dirt that the water becomes turbid.
The nature is fundamentally pure from the beginning; however, because adventitious afflictions cloud the mind and render it turbid, the true nature does not manifest.
If one wishes to prevent such confusion and turbidity, one should take up a rosary and, while reciting, maintain the mind in a single state of focus.

There are many kinds of rosaries: namely, those made of rudrākṣa seeds, lotus seeds, aruḍarācaka seeds, crystal, red copper, tin, wood-apple (kaṇṭhakī) seeds, lapis lazuli, gold, silver, high-carbon steel (bainṛtya), or conch shell; one may choose any one of these materials to serve as a rosary.
Having devoutly taken up the rosary, one should perform the recitation using either the right or left hand.

One should contemplate the mantra, reciting it with single-minded focus without allowing any confusion; one should fix the mind upon the tutelary deity, or reflect upon the mantra along with the mudrās and so forth.

Just as when entering meditative absorption, do not allow the mind to be distracted; with the senses subdued, sit upright before the Honored One. Once the visualization is perfected, move your lips slightly and recite the mantra.

The human mind is as volatile as wind and lightning, like a monkey leaping from tree to tree, or like the surging waves of the ocean; it wanders freely in deviousness and becomes attached to various sensory objects.
Therefore, one must restrain the mind so that it remains unmoving and recite the mantra.

If the mind becomes weary, drowsy, or falls into sleep, or if it is oppressed and confused, one should rise and practice walking meditation, or gaze at the four directions, or sprinkle water on the face to bring about clarity and awakening.

While walking in meditation, one might unexpectedly remember one's former preceptor, or recall deceased parents, or think of fellow students; or, upon reflecting on them, the mind of lust may immediately stir and become unsettled.
The practitioner of recitation should thus examine their own body and mind:
"This body has no master; it wanders through all realms of existence driven by karma, having no place of reliance.
After casting off this body, one again receives another form; thus, the causes of good and evil karma continue without end."

Birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress; the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of encountering what one hates, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—nowhere can one ever escape these.
Mosquitoes, horseflies, fleas, lice, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes, as well as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst—such sufferings as these exist everywhere.
"The various devas have no way to escape together;
even those whose minds wish to retreat and turn toward other directions [shall not do so].
One should employ this gate of contemplation as an antidote.
If greed and hatred are predominant, one should cultivate the contemplation of white bones as well as the various impure contemplations of the bloated, the swollen, the festering, and the decaying;
if the fire of anger is predominant, one should practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion;
if ignorance is predominant, one should practice the contemplation of dependent origination.

Sometimes an enemy turns into a good friend, and sometimes a close friend turns into an enemy. If one approaches them with a mind of equanimity, that very equanimity may further change and turn them into an enemy. Thus, one should observe that these relatives and friends all possess an indeterminate nature.
The wise should not give rise to vain attachments. When the mind desires to go and visit friends or relatives during the interval, one must apply this Dharma-gate as an antidote.

When wishing to recite [the scriptures], or after completing the activities of walking, standing, or lying down, one must not engage in conversation with non-Buddhists, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as eunuchs, boys, girls, virgins, widows, and the like.
When the Dharma service is concluded, if one wishes to speak, one should thereafter engage in discussion on wholesome teachings with one's companions.
Any other miscellaneous talk provides an opportunity for Māra; it is not right discourse.

When sneezing or spitting, one must discard them at a distance; having discarded them, one should immediately rinse the mouth with cleansing powder (*śāṭī*). After performing the relief of the great or small excretions, one must likewise bathe.
One should offer incense, flowers, and lamps as offerings, prostrate before the Buddha, and praise the Triple Gem during the six periods of day and night.
One should always remain humble, give rise to compassion for all sentient beings, and cultivate a mind intent on rescuing them from suffering.
All merits cultivated through such diligent recitation and practice as described above should be dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Just as all rivers flow toward the great ocean, and once they have entered it, they become of one single taste;
so too is the dedication toward Bodhi: all merits are gathered together to collectively accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood.

It is like a person who plows a field and sows rice, seeking only the grain and not hoping for the stalks; once the grain has ripened and been harvested, the stalks are obtained naturally without being sought.

If a practitioner wishes to obtain the merit that is the seed of Bodhi, they should not seek unsurpassed Bodhi for the sake of worldly pleasures; using these as a metaphor for its fruit, how much more so should all other worldly pleasures be regarded as mere grass and stalks, which one does not seek and yet obtains of their own accord?

Regarding worldly pleasures: whether it be among the gods or humans—such as becoming one of the twenty-eight heavenly kings, or becoming a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) in the human realm who rules over the four continents—if there is someone who, seeking minor gain, requests that you feign going there, you should not, for the sake of that person, abandon any of your fundamental vows.
That former person replied to him with these words:

"Wait until I have attained a long-lived body as a fruit [of my practice], and have acquired various other requisites; then, with an insatiable mind, I shall benefit sentient beings and fulfill their various desires and aspirations, after which I will go there."

"There is no need for you to take such pains to request that I go there; I am one of meager merit who speaks with flattery, seeking offerings from others to sustain my life. I would violate the Mantra Secret Teachings by accepting such a wrong livelihood, and since the Buddha gave me no such instruction, I will certainly not comply."
"Furthermore, Suvāhu, youth!

Any who uphold mantras must distance themselves from the eight worldly dharmas: using the good to counteract the reputation for evil, as well as suffering and pleasure, gain and loss, defamation and praise."
These eight worldly dharmas can give rise to all unwholesome states;
for example, just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, such that it will not remain in the sea for even a single moment.
If the practitioner of recitation gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, they should quickly distance themselves from them, ensuring that not even a single thought remains in the mind.
It is like lighting a lamp or candle inside a room: it is solely for the purpose of warding off the wind; because there is no wind, the flame becomes increasingly bright.
"By reciting mantras and further applying diligent effort with courageous and fierce perseverance, causing wholesome dharmas to increase is likewise so.
Furthermore, O youth Subāhu!"

Those who maintain this recitation must always maintain mindfulness throughout the four modes of deportment, ensuring that body and mind do not become frivolous or agitated, thereby losing their resolve and integrity.
One must not clap hands, engage in music, singing, dancing, weddings, or gambling, nor go to witness such activities; furthermore, one must not disparage householders.

Furthermore, one must distance oneself from practicing deceitful speech, speaking of others' long and short faults, sleeping at improper times, engaging in meaningless talk, and studying secular literature or various heterodox teachings. One must also abandon anger, resentment, stinginess, greed, arrogance, negligence, and indolence; likewise, one shall neither drink alcohol nor eat meat.

One should not eat onions, garlic, leeks, sesame, radishes, or *buddhika*—here translated as "donkey-hoof"—nor sesame oil and the like. Furthermore, one must not consume any leftover food, food offered in sacrifices to spirits, or food used for ritual offerings.
As with the aforementioned leftover food, none of these should be eaten.
If one eats such food, they are not called a practitioner of mantras, and their recitation will yield no efficacy.
"Furthermore, O Youth Subāhu!
One should diligently recite day and night without interruption; all invocations and dismissals must be performed according to the Dharma.
When wishing to recite, one should spread *kuśa* grass and sit or lie upon it.

When about to sleep, first practice the contemplations of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; furthermore, with a mind of deep reverence for the Triple Gem and the stūpas containing relics, seek the eradication of transgressions.
If one lies down without performing such contemplative practice, one is not called a practitioner of recitation; it is like lying down with a corpse.
"Furthermore, Su-ba-hu (Subāhu) youth!

The practitioner of recitation should always consume the "three white foods," or eat a mixture of vegetable roots, fruits, milk products including curd and ghee, barley, flour cakes, oil-cakes, and whey; the same applies to various kinds of gruels and porridges.
If one desires to achieve accomplishment, one should eat sesame dregs mixed with curd-milk; by performing this according to the rite, one will certainly obtain the signs of efficacy.
Chapter Four: The Section on the Differentiation of the Vajra-Club and the Signs of Efficacy of Medicines from the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-tantra*. "Furthermore, Subāhu-kumāra!..."

For your sake and for the sake of future sons of good family who resolve to recite the secret mantra-gate, I shall explain the upholding of the Vajra; listen attentively, and having heard it, you should explain it extensively for others.
"If one wishes to fashion a vajra, its length should be eight finger-widths, or ten finger-widths, or twelve finger-widths, or sixteen finger-widths; the maximum length is twenty finger-widths."
If one desires to achieve great nobility and sovereignty, or seeks the siddhi of a vidyādhara, one should fashion a vajra out of gold.
If one seeks wealth and status, one should fashion a vajra made entirely of silver.
"If one wishes to seek the Sea Dragon King, one should fashion a vajra from refined copper.
If one wishes to enter the palace of the asuras, one should use exquisite sandstone to fashion a vajra."
"If one wishes to accomplish all things universally, one should fashion a vajra by combining gold, silver, and copper.
If one wishes to achieve the subjugation of the yakṣa hosts, one should fashion a vajra from iron."
"If one desires to obtain freedom from illness or seeks wealth, one should fashion a vajra from śirīṣa wood or bilva wood."
"If one wishes to cure all diseases or those possessed by malevolent spirits, one should fashion a vajra from khadira wood.
If one wishes to accomplish the rites for yakṣiṇīs, mothers, sisters, or female kin, one should use madhuka wood to fashion the vajra."
"If one wishes to seek the method for extinguishing transgressions, one should fashion a *vajra* from *aśvattha* wood.
If one wishes to employ the method for subduing enemies, one should fashion a *vajra* from wood used for harming others."
"If one wishes to subdue extremely wicked enemies, one should fashion a *vajra* from human bone.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of illusory transformation (*māyā-vidyā*), one should fashion a *vajra* from crystal."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite for causing mutual hatred among people, one should fashion a vajra from *kaṭuka* wood.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite for causing nāga maidens to pay respectful attention, one should fashion a vajra from *nāga* wood."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite for causing beings of the ghost class to wither and engage in strife and contention, one should fashion a *vajra* from *vibhītaka* wood.
If one wishes to accomplish the rites for devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or asuras, one should fashion a *vajra* from celestial wood."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of transforming one's form, one should fashion a vajra out of clay.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of raising a corpse, one should fashion a vajra out of kātan wood."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite for seeking wealth, one may use *arka* wood to fashion a *vajra*, or else use *nāga* wood, or *aśoka* wood; any of these may be employed."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite for subduing adversaries, one may use śrīparṇī wood to fashion a vajra; alternatively, amra wood, aśvattha wood, or willow wood may all be used."
"If one wishes to seek the fulfillment of all desires and aspirations, one may fashion a vajra from white sandalwood, or it may be made from red sandalwood; either is acceptable."
"Regarding the various types of vajra methods described above, each and every one must be fashioned with five prongs; they should be pure, exquisite, and dignified, without any deficiency."

When the practitioner wishes to perform recitation, they should smear the ground with fragrant mud, scatter excellent and beautiful flowers as an offering, generate a mind of great compassion, hold a vajra in their hand, and recite the mantra.
When the ritual service is completed, one should again make offerings, placing the vajra upon the feet of the deity; this is likewise to be done during subsequent recitations.
If one performs recitation without grasping the sublime vajra, one will ultimately not achieve accomplishment.
Why is this? Because malevolent spirits do not fear [the rite] and benevolent deities do not bestow their protection, all ritual matters will find it difficult to achieve their intended efficacy.
If one is unable to fashion a vajra, one must instead form that mudrā; thereafter, by reciting with single-minded devotion according to the Dharma, one shall likewise attain accomplishment.
Do not give rise to negligence and waste your efforts; it would be better to cultivate other practices instead.
"Furthermore, Sūbhūti the Youth!
For those who recite mantras and accomplish medicinal rites, there are seventeen kinds of substances in total:

"First, realgar; second, ox-gallstone; third, yellow arsenic; fourth, *añjana*; fifth, cinnabar; sixth, *dhūta* incense; seventh, *vajra*; eighth, cow’s ghee; ninth, *kṣīraka* (achyranthes); tenth, *maunakelikā*; eleventh, garments; twelfth, a trident; thirteenth, deer skin; fourteenth, a horizontal sword; fifteenth, a lasso; sixteenth, armor; seventeenth, a trident."
"All the items mentioned above possess these three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Even if there are other items for accomplishment described within the teachings of other mantra methods, they do not deviate from these three types."
Regarding matters that are temporarily pleasing, one may act as one wishes; there shall be none who fail to attain their desired results.
"Furthermore, Suvāhu, the youth!

There are various obstacles and vināyakas in the world who, seeking out faults, constantly look for an opportunity against those who recite mantras. Within this context, one must carefully attend to the matter, employing skillful means and wisdom to discern and understand it well."
How many factions are there in total within the host of Māra?
To speak of them collectively, there are four factions. What are these four?
"First is the *Cūḍāmaṇi* (Crest-Jewel) section; second, the *Vajra* (Thunderbolt) section;
third, the *Ekadanta* (Single-Tusked) section; and fourth, the *Nāgendra* (Dragon-Elephant) section.
From these four sections flow forth immeasurable hosts of *vināyakas*, which are listed in full below:"
"The leader of the Crushing Division is named Great General; within his division are various types of forms, and he has seven asaṃkhyeyas as his retinue."
Regarding the mantras spoken by the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, those who recite them will constantly encounter obstacles and difficulties caused by their kind.

Within the division known as the Wild Division (Kṣetrapāla), there is one named Elephant Head; among his followers, whose forms are difficult to fully describe, there are eighteen koṭis serving as his retinue.
Regarding the mantras spoken by the Heavenly King Maheśvara, those who maintain and recite them will constantly encounter obstacles and hindrances from that class of beings.
Within this family, there is a Lord of the Single Tusk named Bhīṣaṇajaṭa; among his various forms and terrifying countenances, he has one hundred and forty koṭis of retinues as his followers.

Regarding the mantras spoken by Mahābrahmā, the mantras spoken by Kauśika, the Sun and Moon Devas, Nārāyaṇa Deva, and the various Vāyu Devas: there are those who maintain and recite them, yet various classes of beings constantly create obstacles and difficulties for them.
"The leader of the dragon-elephant host is named Śikhaṇḍin; within his host there are various forms of unknown names, and he has one koṭi-nayuta of one thousand padma as his retinue."
Regarding those who maintain and recite the profound and subtle mantras taught in the Śākya teachings, they will constantly create obstacles and difficulties for them.
Furthermore, regarding those who maintain and recite the mantras spoken by Pañcika, known as the son of Hariṇegameṣi, he will create obstacles and difficulties for them.
"Furthermore, Maṇibhadra has a son named Pūrṇabhadra; for those who recite the mantras taught within the Maṇi section, he creates obstacles and difficulties."

"Such classes of vināyakas each create obstacles within their respective families, taking no pleasure in the cultivation of the path and preventing the practitioner who upholds the mantra from attaining accomplishment."
Having manifested as the primary mantra-lord himself, he came to the recitation hall of the human practitioner to receive offerings.
At that time, the Lord of Radiance (Vidyārāja), having witnessed this event, immediately returned to his own palace.
They form this thought:
"How is it that the Tathāgata permits such vows to disturb those who recite mantras, causing their practice to fail and creating such obstacles?"

Even if Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas, nāgas, and others cannot overcome those obstacles created by the Vināyakas, the practitioner should maintain a firm mind and advance with resolve, making a great vow: "The Blessed One has taught the teachings of the Great Vidyā-mantras; I shall now practice according to the Dharma and must overcome these obstacles."
Therefore, once the practitioner of recitation has completed the required number of repetitions, they should further construct the sublime maṇḍala for accomplishing all matters.
Having performed this rite, those who create obstacles will immediately disperse and dare not remain.

"Furthermore, Subāhu, if a practitioner of recitation does not receive the instructions of a teacher, or if they maintain the mantras and perform offerings and homa rituals without following the teachings of the Dharma, those various māras will immediately find an opportunity to create obstacles and difficulties. They cause the practitioner’s mind to be constantly wavering, giving rise to doubt in every thought:
'Should I recite this vidyā-mantra, or that one? "

When he forms such a thought, the opponent finds an opportunity; they immediately speak much that is meaningless, discuss worldly matters, or speak of commerce, or agriculture, or debate fame and profit, causing his mind to become distracted.
For example, it is like a person walking along the water; their reflection enters the water, and the body and its shadow follow one another, never parting.
It is just the same with those Vināyakas and others who enter the bodies of those performing recitation; they are constantly inseparable from them.
Furthermore, there are *vināyakas* who gain entry into the body at the time of bathing;
some *vināyakas* gain entry while one is correctly reciting mantras;
and some *vināyakas* gain entry while the person reciting is fast asleep.
There are *vināyakas* who, when one is performing the proper offerings, find an opportunity to enter one’s body.

Just as fire emerges from a sun-crystal when it is struck by sunlight, so too do *vināyakas* enter the body of the practitioner; likewise, at the time of recitation, they cause the mind to become distracted and increase the fires of greed, delusion, and ignorance.

Furthermore, there is a vināyaka named Jalacara (Water-Walker). If there is any deficiency in the ritual while one is bathing, he seizes the opportunity to enter the body of the practitioner, causing various ailments to arise, namely: hunger and thirst, coughing, indolence, excessive sleep, heaviness of the four limbs, and unprovoked anger.

Furthermore, there is a *vināyaka* named Gandhabhakṣa (Eater of Fragrance). If there is a deficiency in the ritual when offering scented ointments, that māra enters the body and causes the practitioner to fall ill. Specifically, he causes the practitioner to give rise to thoughts and recollections of places from which they originated; or to think of other places; or to think of widows, thereby giving rise to indolence;
or to think of former haunts of sensual indulgence, causing them to abandon their spiritual practice;

or to think of how they formerly squandered vast wealth, indulged in wine and meat, consorted with courtiers, distinguished between the noble and the lowly, observed various sensory objects, and craved beautiful desires, thereby retreating from the resolve for the Path.

Furthermore, there is a Vināyaka named Dīpaśikha (Lamp-Crest). If there is any deficiency in the ritual when offering lamps and fire, he seizes the opportunity to enter the body, causing various illnesses to arise in the practitioner, namely: heart pain, high fever, and injury to the heart.

Furthermore, there is a Vināyaka named Hāsagandha (Laughing Fragrance). If there is any deficiency in the ritual when flowers are being offered, he seizes the opportunity and causes various obstacles to arise for the practitioner of recitation, namely: high fever, nasal congestion, sneezing, tears flowing from the eyes, aching in the limbs and bones, as well as quarreling with one's companions and their subsequent dispersal.

"Furthermore, there is a vināyaka named Vyaghraketu; if there is any deficiency in the dharma of one who is correctly reciting, he seizes the opportunity and causes various ailments to arise in that reciter, namely high fever, and the inability to pass urine or feces."

"When various *vināyakas* enter the body, they cause the mind to become deluded, perceiving west as east and south as north, manifesting various strange signs; or one may begin to chant verses, or desire to wander about for no reason, harboring heterodox thoughts and indecision, which leads to the arising of false views. One then speaks thus:
'There are no mantras of great majesty, nor is there a heavenly realm, nor are there good or evil, nor is there bondage or liberation.
One claims that the practitioner's recitation is a waste of effort, thereby giving rise to false views, becoming separated from the wholesome, and repudiating cause and effect."
He cuts grass with his hands and plays with clods of earth; when sleeping, he gnashes his teeth.

He may give rise to thoughts of desire or wish to take a wife; those whom he loves do not love him in return, and those whom he does not like he finds pleasing. Since things do not accord with his wishes, he lies there unable to sleep, desiring to go and violate the wives and children of others.

His mind is restless and he cannot sleep; even if he should fall asleep, he dreams of being pursued by tigers, lions, leopards, wolves, pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, cats, ghosts, jackals, vultures, herons, cranes, and *ṛkṣa* bears.

At times he dreams of seeing people dressed in old, tattered, and impure clothing; at times he dreams of seeing people who are naked, bald-headed, and dark-complexioned; or he dreams of seeing naked non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); or he sees dried-up ponds and dried-up wells; or he sees skulls; or he sees heaps of bones; or he sees ruined and abandoned houses and dwellings; or he sees grinding stones; or he sees terrifying, evil men holding spears, swords, and various weapons, intending to come and harm him.
Upon seeing such evil omens, one should know that those *vināyakas* are creating obstacles.

The practitioners should immediately perform self-protection using the mantra of the wrathful Vidyārāja Cundī and the *māra-vidrāvaṇa-mudrā*; thus, all the various demonic obstacles mentioned above will be completely extinguished and unable to cause disturbance.
If there are those who recite that mantra, no *vināyakas* shall ever find an opportunity to harm them.
Furthermore, O youth Subāhu!

If a practitioner of recitation wishes to rescue those who are attached to obstacles and bring them to liberation, they should go to a place where herds of cattle dwell, or beneath a single tree, or within a shrine, or at a crossroads, or in a secluded room, or in a forest. Having obtained one of such locations as described above, they may select a site according to their preference; once the ritual for preparing the ground is completed, they should take cow dung mixed with scented water and smear it upon the ground. Once it has dried, they should again smear the ground with scented water, and then apply five-colored earth, following the rules for the *maṇḍala* using these five colors.
The altar is square, measuring three cubits in width, and is provided with four gates.

Within it, a pit two cubits square is constructed; inside the pit, *kuśa* grass is spread. Outside the pit, at each of the two-cubit intervals, seats are arranged for the placement of the Vidyārājas and Mantra-lords, while the great deities of their respective directions are painted in the eight cardinal points.

Furthermore, take four new jars—none of which should be black, over-fired, or raw—and fill them to the brim with scented water, along with the five precious gems, red lotuses, and various fragrant herbs and flowers; all these shall serve as offerings.
Insert the tender branches of fruit trees and other such items into the necks of the vases, which should be bound with threads of five colors and placed in the four directions.
Thereafter, one should invite those vidyārājas and others, and worship them with various ritual offerings.
Furthermore, with wine, meat, radishes, and many varieties of *pāloraka* food, he made offerings to those great deities of the eight directions and to all the *vināyakas*.
Having placed that person who is attached to obstacles into the pit, have them sit facing east.

The practitioner, sitting on the western side of the maṇḍala facing east, shall recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, taking the water from the four vases placed at the corners, he shall recite the mantras of Amṛtakuṇḍalin (translated here as the Red-colored Vidyārāja), Kīlikīla Vidyārāja, and Nāramiḷana Vidyārāja more than one hundred and eight times, and then perform the consecration upon their heads.
These four vases should be poured out in succession; having performed this rite, those possessed by obstructing spirits will immediately attain liberation.

This maṇḍala is not only able to remove all *vināyakas*, but can also benefit those involved in legal affairs, women who have difficulty marrying, merchants who fail to obtain profit from their trade, farmers who do not harvest grain, those possessed by *piśācas*, children suffering from high fevers, those possessed by malevolent spirits, those who fall prey to *graha* spirits that suck vitality or exhale poison, those who constantly see evil dreams while sleeping at night, those afflicted by epilepsy, and those with the ten types of diseases and so forth.

By performing this maṇḍala and bestowing that empowerment, all beings of every kind shall obtain benefit; whatever they seek shall be fully satisfied, all other ailments shall likewise be cured, and furthermore, immeasurable karmic obstacles shall be extinguished.

Chapter Five: The Section on the Characteristics of the Accomplishment of Discrimination Furthermore, Suvāhu,
when that practitioner has attained liberation from all obstacles and difficulties, his body and mind become pure, free from all defilements and impurities.
It is, for example, like the bright moon buried within clouds; when the clouds are dispelled and vanish, it shines beautifully in the radiant sky, manifesting clearly within the void.

In the same way, the various merits cultivated by one who recites mantras eliminate and sever all obstacles and difficulties created by Vināyakas, causing them to be entirely extinguished; likewise, all the mantras they maintain will attain accomplishment.

It is like a seed that, depending upon the earth, the season, and the irrigation of rain, becomes moistened and well-conditioned; then, obtaining favorable winds and rain, it subsequently sprouts and eventually reaches maturity.
However, if the seed remains within the granary, even a sprout will not emerge, let alone branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit.

Likewise, if one recites mantras without following the ritual rules, fails to perform offerings, or because one is already impure; or if the syllables of the mantra are added or subtracted, or the phonetic characteristics are incorrect, one will similarly fail to attain the vast and wondrous siddhis.
For example, when clouds arise and rain falls, the amount that descends corresponds to the merit of sentient beings;
likewise, the accomplishments attained by one who recites this mantra correspond to the labor they have exerted.

If there is a practitioner who, in a pure place, according to the time and seasonal regulations prescribed by the Dharma, causes whatever transgressions have been committed to gradually diminish, fulfills the accumulation of merit, and is able to obtain the empowerment and accomplishment of the mantra.
If one's transgressions are not extinguished and one's merits are not perfected, and if one does not conform to the ritual rules, the mantra will not be accomplished;
the opposite of this should be understood. "Furthermore, Suvāhu, the youth!

If the practitioner commits any transgressions during the recitation, or if there are interruptions—such as abandoning the original mantra being recited to hold another vidyā, or bestowing one's own mantra upon others—the count of recitations will not be accomplished even if the total number is reached. Furthermore, one must once again perform ritual offerings according to the Dharma at the three times each day until the number of recitations reaches one hundred thousand, at which point one should perform the homa offering according to the Dharma.

One should take either barley, rice blossoms, sesame seeds, or white mustard seeds; taking any one of these and mixing it with clarified butter, one should recite the mantra four thousand times, or seven or eight thousand times.

"Whether it be udumbara wood, or aśvattha wood, or palāśa wood, or agaru wood, or nāga wood, or aśoka wood, or milupa wood, or nyagrodha wood, or āmra wood, or khadira wood, or śamīka wood, or plakṣa wood, or apāmārga wood, or maduka wood, or momu-ka wood—among these various woods mentioned above, take whichever one you please. These four aggregates should be known as empty: form is impermanent like a mass of foam; feeling is like a floating bubble; perception is like a mirage; formations are like a plantain tree; and consciousness is like a magical illusion. Chapter Seven: The Section on the Signs of Siddhi. *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*. "Furthermore, Subāhu, the youth!..."

"What you have said is so; listen with a profound and attentive mind.

This body is a provisional formation through the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind, like four venomous snakes placed within a single basket.

The practitioner, upon those objects, should again sprinkle scented water for a brief moment and perform one thousand homa offerings according to the appropriate rite.

The preceding passage refers to those who have attained the first *siddhi* of "warmth.

If one wishes to see one’s own body attain mastery at will, sitting upon the thrones of devas and humans to preach the Dharma for the assembly—for whether it be for a small kalpa, a great kalpa, or immeasurable kalpas—so that the teaching of all dharmas remains uninterrupted, benefiting sentient beings without end, and seeking such eloquence in order to succeed to the rank of a Bodhisattva.

It is like a person who has died and whose body is entirely cold, yet who then attains the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and enters the body again, subsequently reviving and living for a hundred years.

the eight sufferings shall all cease, and they shall attain the Eightfold Noble Path;
the nine afflictions shall be stilled, and they shall attain the nine successive meditative absorptions.

"If one sees such signs as these, it should be reported that one will certainly attain *siddhi* without doubt.
One should immediately prepare incense and flowers, fill a pure vessel with scented water, and place within it the five precious gems; this shall be respectfully offered as *argha*."

Immediately, with a profound mind of reverence, he knelt on his right knee and bowed his head; measuring his own prior efforts against the fruits of his aspirations, he spoke these words as they had been taught by that Honored One:

Chapter Eight: The Section on the Lower *Bhasman* (Ashes). From the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*. "Furthermore, Subāhu, the youth!..."

In such a place, once the lower-ranking *pāṃśula* spirits have been summoned, they shall immediately speak for themselves regarding matters of the heavens and the human world, as well as the past, future, and present—transcending the three periods of time—including all matters of good and evil, explaining each one in full detail.

If there is a deficiency in the ritual, if the number of mantra syllables is increased or decreased, if it has not been recited, if right faith is lacking and no offerings are made, if the ground is impure and the deities are not clear and bright, or if the body parts of the youth are either redundant or deficient.
