Next, one should immediately make offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, unguents, burning incense, and various kinds of food and drink to the principal deity, as well as to the great deities who guard the eight directions and the various classes of asuras and other spirits; each and every one must be offered to.

Furthermore, one should scatter exquisite flowers upon the body of that youth and anoint his body with incense; thereafter, the practitioner who performs the recitation, holding an incense burner in hand, prostrates to the Honored One and recites the mantra.
First, place the syllable *hūṃ*; in the middle, one should utter the phrase *kṛṣṇa*; then utter *abhiśa*, which means "pervading entry"; and then utter *kṣepa*, which means "swift."

When one has descended into *sīna*, these signs immediately appear: the eyes are joyful, one gazes at objects without blinking, and there is no inhalation or exhalation; one should then know that one has descended into *sīna*.
Immediately take *argha* water and incense as offerings, and while reciting the mantra of the Supreme Vidyārāja in one's mind, one should respectfully inquire:
"Venerable One, what kind of deity are you? If there is any doubt regarding oneself or others, one should ask immediately."
"He shall himself explain matters of the three periods of time, such as gain and loss of profit, suffering and pleasure, and so forth.
You should promptly receive and uphold the teachings you hear; do not give rise to doubt."
Once the matters you have heard are concluded, dispatch [the messenger] immediately.
If you possess this method, Piṇā will descend swiftly; if you do not act according to the ritual, you will not achieve success and will be ridiculed by others.

Furthermore, regarding those who are *sina* by nature: those youths have faces that are joyful and radiant, with complexions that are moist and lustrous; their eyes are wide and long, with a slight reddish hue encircling the black pupils; they possess the physical marks of a great man, such as having no inhalation or exhalation and not blinking their eyes—one should know that such individuals are truly *sina*.

If the māras and others appear inferior, they will have distinct characteristics: their eyes are red and round like those of a person looking on in anger; the pupils do not move; they gape with terror and lack inhalation or exhalation; and their eyes do not blink. One should then know that these are yakṣas and the like, and must be dispatched.
If they are unwilling to depart, one should immediately recite the verses of Mañjuśrī, or recite the mantra of the Impure Wrathful Vajra, or read the Mahāsannipāta-dhāraṇī-sūtra.

If, after reciting as described above, [the obstacle] does not depart, one should immediately perform a fire offering (*homa*) one hundred and eight times using *arka* water mixed with *palāśa* wood and clarified butter (*sarpis*), reciting the Siṃhāsana mantra; or, using sesame seeds or rice-ear flowers mixed with clarified butter and honey, perform a fire offering one hundred times; finally, perform a fire offering seven or three times with the Kuntali mantra, and it will immediately depart.
The wise person who skillfully understands such sublime Dharma and is further able to practice it accordingly, one by one, will achieve accomplishment before long, without excessive toil.
Chapter Nine: The Section on Distinguishing Obstacles and Difficulties From the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra* Furthermore, Subāhu, the youth!

There may be a practitioner of recitation who, in the past, killed an Arhat; in this present life, has committed rebellion against his parents; has disrupted the harmony of the Sangha; and, out of a mind of hatred, has shed the blood of a Buddha.

Due to the influence of evil habitual tendencies, they now seek out the faults of others; when their own minds encounter matters, they lack proficiency yet falsely assume an air of understanding. Such people do not meet with virtuous friends.

Due to associating with evil friends, they instead give rise to false views; furthermore, they destroy stūpas, kill bodhisattvas who are destined for enlightenment (*niyata*), defile the mother of an arhat, instruct others to kill, or steal monastic property—whether much or little. The World-Honored One declares these to be persons guilty of the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

If one commits [any of these], the offense increases by one fold; if one commits all five heinous crimes (ānantarya), it increases fivefold. At the end of life, such a person shall enter the Avīci Hell and undergo suffering for ten great kalpas.

Furthermore, there are those who manifest in physical form yet commit boundless sins; with minds clouded by ignorance and arrogance, they refuse to confess their transgressions. Instead, they give rise to the view of self and seek to recite and uphold the secret treasury of mantras. Even if they labor diligently in the recitation of mantras, they will ultimately fail to attain *siddhi*.

Because their hindrances are heavy; because they have not yet confessed and apologized for their transgressions before another person; because they have not yet repaid debts owed to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, or the property of all spiritual teachers and friends; and because they have not yet reformed even a hair’s breadth of their reckless, obstinate, and ignorant ways—how can they possibly recite mantras and seek to attain the fruit of siddhi?
The four realms of existence are long and far-reaching; once one has fallen into them, when will there ever be deliverance and liberation?

If all these classes of suffering beings were not those who had not yet undergone the karma of the evil destinies, the Blessed One would not have spoken of the existence of icchantikas or the sufferings of hell and so forth.

What is the explanation? One must seek liberation with diligence, and strive for *siddhi* through asceticism and the mortification of the body. Furthermore, regarding the subtle and wondrous sutras spoken by the Buddhas:

if one destroys them out of a mind of hatred, or burns them with fire, or discards them in water, or casts them into an impure latrine; or if one slanders the Dharma-body; or if one kills a precept-observing bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā; or if one intends to beat, revile, deceive, or insult them, using evil words to slander and defame them, seeking out their faults; or if one carries fire to burn a monastery or vihāra, destroying honored guests or the monastic quarters—such persons, when their retribution is exhausted and their lives end, shall fall into all the Avīci hells throughout the ten directions, where they shall endure suffering for a thousand kalpas.
Thereafter, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); once their existence as ghosts has ended, they again fall among the animals (*tiryagyoni*).

Once their existence as animals has ended, they finally obtain a human body, yet their six sense faculties are incomplete, and they are always born into lowly families, living as beggars. Even if they possess physical strength, they constantly seek wealth by carrying corpses for hire to sustain their lives; their food and drink do not suffice for their mouths, and they perpetually suffer from hunger, consuming food and drink without discrimination, or even eating the flesh of dogs, pigs, cats, rats, and the like to sustain their lives.

If one encounters virtuous friends, one immediately gives rise to bodhicitta; however, if one meets those such as icchantikas or the ignorant, one again commits evil karma and falls back into hell for many kalpas.
As the World-Honored One has taught, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in turn make offerings to the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because they seek merit.
How much more so for ordinary people, who devote themselves exclusively to stubborn folly and fail to seek merit?

The Bodhisattva, out of compassion for sentient beings, attains the Buddha-body; he does not abandon any sentient being, and those who see him gaze upon him with reverent mindfulness, never tiring of it.
A bodhisattva does not harm the life of even a single sentient being, much less many lives.
Because they do not cause harm, they attain a body free from all suffering of illness and endowed with all perfections.
After attaining Buddhahood, his lifespan further increased.
It is the same with the gift of food: one obtains a long life.
When sentient beings encounter the shadow of the Buddha, they all attain peace and happiness, and their lives and bodies are preserved.
A bodhisattva always remains humble toward sentient beings, receiving and honoring them; if they have any need, the bodhisattva does not contradict their wishes but provides everything they require.

If the person before him understands the Dharma, the bodhisattva offers his own body, bed, and seat for them to sit upon, so that they may listen to the sublime Dharma and practice it accordingly, never regressing and seeking the eternal body of a Buddha—how much more so for an ordinary person who understands nothing and possesses not a hair’s breadth of merit, yet treats all with contempt, indulges in arrogance, and fails to follow the wise in practicing the karma of giving (*dāna*) and its fruits?

"Now, I shall briefly explain the two categories of transgression and merit. A person who has committed a transgression must first seek repentance, confessing their faults face-to-face and describing each one in detail; for if they conceal them and fail to describe them, the transgression will be difficult to extinguish.
Thereafter, they should seek out a skilled and enlightened master, honoring and supporting them with reverence and looking up to them with esteem, and request entry into the *samaya* dharma."
Once you have received permission and entered the maṇḍala, you should subsequently inquire gradually into the rules of the mantra. Having mastered them, through practice you shall attain siddhi.
Those who lack a virtuous mind merely waste their words and efforts; only the torments of hell can turn such people back.
"Furthermore, Suvāhu, the youth!
If a practitioner of recitation first arouses a mind of reverence, humility, and obedience toward the Triple Gem, and then kneels before them with palms joined, addresses the Venerable One, saying:
'I now repent of all my karmic obstructions; may they be entirely extinguished. From this day forward, I shall not commit them again.'"

We pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept us; having resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhi within the Buddha-dharma, until we reach Buddhahood, may we not encounter evil Māras who would destroy our true vision of bodhi.

May the World-Honored One bear witness: from this day forward, I shall never again return to other demons, heterodox teachers, or evil persons, nor shall I prostrate before various classes of worldly deities; I shall fix my mind upon the Buddha, Bodhi, and the Triple Gem alone, vowing never to waver for even a single thought-moment.
When one makes such vows as these, the ritual methods for recitation and mantra-chanting will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
One will also be able to rescue and gather sentient beings, taking their suffering and afflictions upon oneself in their stead.
Regarding all things required by the assembly, although my merit is meager, I shall provide for them according to my ability so that they are fully satisfied.

By the power of my resolve for bodhicitta and my recitation of mantras, may I subdue those human beings who are fierce, harmful, and malicious; may they be unable to cause harm and naturally perish, and may all sentient beings be entirely free from fear.

Now, because I recite with a sincere heart and all the celestial deities and benevolent spirits provide protection, the power of the mantra is inconceivable; all spirits revere it and are struck with awe. How much more so for ordinary people and evildoers—how could they not be subdued and destroyed?

"Furthermore, any practitioner who upholds a mantra must not, without cause, cut grass or trees with their hands; nor should they tread upon lotuses, various ritual grounds, or mudrās with their feet; nor should they prostrate before medicinal herbs and the like.
They must not consume food offered as an oblation or used in sacrifices to spirits and deities, nor eat food that has been discarded or placed on the ground.
They must not converse with women or with animals."

To perform non-dharmic acts in a pure place—such as catching various snakes by means of mantras or medicinal herbs, or riding an elephant or a live donkey to make it run, or striking it with a staff until it falls ill and encounters hardship—and to fail to give rise to thoughts of compassion toward those who suffer: such a person will find it difficult to achieve accomplishment even when reciting mantras, and is not called a wise person.
Just as space can never be measured,
so too is it with the performance of benefit or harm toward the Triple Gem and sentient beings, and the subsequent attainment of good or evil retribution.

Furthermore, one must not employ nets, snares, traps, or various other means to harm sentient beings, nor keep cats, wildcats, or black sheep, nor confine parrots and other birds in cages; for such a person, neither in this life nor in future lives will the recitation of mantras achieve accomplishment.

Therefore, one should not make use of offerings intended for the World-Honored One; nor should one tread upon the food offered to him, for food that has fallen to the ground by being stepped upon is unfit to be an offering.

One should not carry it upon the crown of the head, nor should one prostrate before Maheśvara, nor the gods of the Sun and Moon, nor Agni, nor Nārāyaṇa. Even if one should encounter suffering, one should not pay homage to them; nor should one recite their teachings, nor offer worship to them.

If there are those who recite the mantras of that deity, the practitioner should likewise not give rise to anger toward them; rather, they should simply refrain from rejoicing in such acts. One should instead cultivate compassion for those who have fallen into false views, and one must neither recite their mantras nor praise their virtues.
If one possesses wealth and makes offerings, one should, out of compassion, form the aspiration that all sentient beings may abide in right view.

Having made such a vow, whatever action one performs, one should first prostrate to all Buddhas and their abodes, and subsequently pay homage to the assembly of all Vajra protectors of the Dharma and virtuous deities.

For example, although the new moon is not yet full, all people nevertheless pay it homage and prostrate; likewise, those who practice recitation must always revere Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Vajras, and the assembly of Śrāvakas. Although they have not yet awakened to fullness, they will gradually attain the full moon of Bodhi.
Therefore, one must pay homage and prostrate to all the bodhisattvas and the assembly of noble ones.

Those bodhisattvas are able to bear the burden of all sentient beings; because they have given rise to great compassion for the sake of their salvation and have brought it to full maturity, there exists a class of ignorant and inferior beings. From this [teaching] emerges the inconceivable supernormal power and the treasury of mantras endowed with great diligence.
If one does not prostrate, not only will the mantras fail to be accomplished, but one will also slander the Buddhas.

For example, just as fruit is produced from flowers—where the flower represents the Bodhisattva and the fruit symbolizes Bodhi—one must therefore pay homage and take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Although a bodhisattva may engage in desire, manifesting the practice of desire; may manifest toughness toward those who are tough; and may manifest gentle compassion toward those who are gentle—nevertheless, that bodhisattva is free from both hatred and attachment.

Why should one not pay homage to those bodhisattvas? Because they fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings according to their respective types by practicing various mantra methods, and because they are further able to understand all karmic fruits; therefore, one should pay homage to these venerable masters.

10. Chapter on the Analysis of the Factors of the Path.
"Furthermore, Suvāhu, I shall now explain for the practitioner of recitation the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path:
right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is the path traversed by all Buddhas."

For those practitioners who recite [the mantra] and follow this path, the mantra will be accomplished; when their retribution here is exhausted, they shall be reborn in superior and wondrous realms among humans and devas.
Because the Buddhas of the past followed this path, they attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment; the Buddhas of the present and future do likewise.

The merit cultivated through the actions of body, speech, and mind, which is constantly based on the true teaching without giving rise to weariness and practiced with such intent, is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
To always maintain contentment regarding food, clothing, bedding, and the acceptance of medicinal decoctions, without giving rise to defiled attachment, is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).

Not praising oneself, not disparaging others, remaining far removed from all faults as one would avoid a pit of fire or a fierce beast, and always delighting in tranquility—this is called right speech.

One does not study divination of good and bad fortune, the characteristics of men and women, astronomy, geography, the training of hawks, the training of horses, as well as the training of elephants, the arts of archery, calligraphy, and arithmetic, nor any worldly discourses or useless treatises; to remain far removed from such faults is called right discernment.

One does not watch elephant fights, horse fights, or the fighting of oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, and so forth; nor does one go to watch men and women boxing or wrestling. To be free from such spectacles as these is called right mindfulness.

One should not speak of kings, ministers, thieves, battles, mutual slaughter, or discourse concerning courtesans and riddles; rather, one should recount stories of the past. From the time one begins the recitation until its completion, one must not enter cities, villages, towns, or hamlets, nor go to places where monasteries or *caityas* stand, nor to the abodes of non-Buddhist shrines, nor to such places as gardens, groves, ponds, or rivers; one should not visit any of these locations.

If one does not commit the seven types of transgressions mentioned above, but constantly dwells in mountain forests, on high and precipitous peaks, or at the summits of isolated heights, reciting mantras day and night without slackening, there is no fruit that will not be attained; this is called right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
"Furthermore, young Suvāhu!

If a practitioner of recitation does not attain the aforementioned sublime and superior states, they should dwell in a deserted shrine, or beneath a tree, or by a riverbank, or on a mountainside, or among springs, ponds, and forests, or in a solitary place, or in an empty room, and recite with single-minded devotion. Alternatively, during the year—excluding the period of the rains retreat—they may travel at will during the two seasons of spring and autumn, reciting with focused attention in mountain forests, by rivers, at springs and ponds, or in empty rooms, just as a bhikṣu observes the summer rains retreat; the practitioner of recitation should likewise do so."

Although the practitioner may have completed the full number of recitations, one must not perform rites of accomplishment during the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Even if such rites are not performed, the recitation must not be interrupted. Only after concluding the retreat and having properly protected oneself according to the Dharma may one perform rites of accomplishment; be careful never to act outside the prescribed ritual framework.
"Furthermore, Su-ba-hu youth!
I shall now explain for the practitioner of recitation the methods for constructing the homa fire-pit and the distinctions regarding its placement.

This pit may be made circular, triangular, square, or in the shape of a lotus; it must all have a foundation, with a rim installed at the mouth of the pit, smoothed and polished with mud, and the outer foundation and steps must all be firm and stable."
"If one performs virtuous deeds or seeks wealth, and intends for others to regard them with reverence and perform rites for averting calamity, the hearth must be circular.
If one seeks the accomplishment of all matters, or seeks women and young girls, the hearth must be in the shape of a lotus."
"If one performs the *abhicāra* rite, or for purposes such as causing flight and the like, the hearth must be made triangular.

If one wishes to subjugate various *nāgas* and other classes of spirits, or to cause them to be burned by fire, or to cause them suffering, the hearth must be square; its base, rim, and interior should be smeared with *gomaya*. Furthermore, one should spread *kuśa* grass upon the base and beneath it. At the places where it has been smeared, one should apply fragrant flowers and the like, and offer whatever materials have been prepared to the Three Jewels, the presiding deity of the respective family (*kula*), and the various *vidyārājas* and their primary mantra-lords."

When fire is produced in the hearth, one should not blow upon it with the mouth; rather, one should fan the fire with a fan. Then, taking rice-pollen mixed with clarified butter, or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, one should perform *homa* seven, eight, ten, or even twenty-one times while reciting the mantra of the *Vidyeśvara* of one's own *kula*, thereby making offerings to the *Vidyeśvara*.

The practitioner shall sit facing east, take ghee, honey, curd, and so forth, and place them together in a single vessel. Taking *homa* wood, he shall dip both ends into the vessel and cast them into the fire-pit to burn.

In this manner, as the sun and moon do not cease their course, after seven days, or three weeks, four weeks, five weeks, six weeks, or seven weeks; or after one month, or a hundred days, or one hundred and twenty days, the signs of verification will manifest.

"If the practice is not successful through the aforementioned methods, one may set a term based on years—three years, six years, ten years, or twelve years—and once one does not regress from the practice, one will ultimately attain the Great Siddhi."
When performing the homa according to the Dharma during the proper rite of burning the fire, one should observe the color of the flames.
Within the hearth, the colors, sparks, and sounds of the fire will combine; whether the rite is successful or not, its respective signs will manifest of their own accord.

That fire is smokeless, with flames like the color of gold, curling to the right in graceful spirals; the peaks of the flames blaze intensely, their colors sometimes white, sometimes red, or the flames are extremely crimson, as lustrous as the color of coral. The flames surge upward and then flow downward in broad sheets, resembling the light of the sun or moon.

The shapes of the flames take the forms of vases, banners, parasols, and the auspicious *svastika*; they appear like conch shells, lotuses, or sacrificial ladles for clarified butter (*ājya*); they resemble three-pronged or five-pronged vajras, horizontal swords, bundles of grass, or the shape of a chariot.

It may sound like the buzzing of flies, or like the sounds of flutes, *pi*, or *li* pipes; or it may be like the sound of a conch shell. Upon obtaining such various sounds, its fragrance will be like that of burning ghee, yet without being acrid or pungent. The fire will ignite spontaneously without being fanned. When such signs appear, one shall certainly attain vast *siddhi*.

Furthermore, regarding the method for observing the signs of failure when burning the fire: at the time of actually burning the fire, there may be excessive smoke or it may be fiercely violent; its flames are difficult to ignite, and even if they do ignite, they do not grow intense. Later, they suddenly extinguish as if there were no fire at all. The color of the flames is withered and black like dark clouds, shaped like a *palaśa* leaf, or like a trident, a winnowing basket, a male organ, or a bull’s horn. The sound produced by the fire is like the braying of a donkey, and furthermore, sparks leap out and burn the practitioner performing the recitation. The incense smoke within the hearth smells like the stench of a cremated corpse. When such signs appear, it is difficult for the practitioner performing the recitation to attain *siddhi*.
"When the practitioner sees such inauspicious signs, they should immediately perform a homa using the mantras of the Red-Body Vidyārāja, or Kīlikīla, or the impure wrathful Vidyārājas."
Those inauspicious signs shall be extinguished; this must be done according to the Dharma and not treated lightly.
The practitioner must take care never to shave the hair of the three places, nor should they cause it to fall by burning with fire, applying medicinal ointments, or pulling it out with the hands.
For example, it is like a person holding a golden blade in their hand; if they do not know how to grasp and wield it properly, they will surely injure themselves.

Likewise, a mantra practitioner who does not follow the ritual rules, whose lust is rampant, and who displays the hair from the three places to women while generating thoughts of desire—not only will the mantra fail to take effect, but it will be like wielding a sharp blade that brings harm upon one's own body.

Even if the practitioner of recitation does not follow the ritual rules, the Lords of the Family, the Vidyārājas, and the Lords of Mantras are all Bodhisattvas who ultimately do no harm to others. It is only their attendants and retinues who inflict harm when they perceive a transgression. Therefore, one must be cautious and upright; do not commit improper or contrary acts that will bring calamity upon oneself.
"Furthermore, Su-ba-hu, the youth!

If there are those who recite mantras, or who desire to achieve accomplishments and perform various rites, seeking *siddhi* without obstacles, they should offer all kinds of food and drink as sacrifices to the devas, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, and so forth; to the garuḍas, jīvañjīvakas, kaṭapūtanas, gandharvas, bhūtas, and all manner of malevolent spirits—whether they dwell upon the earth or roam through the sky—and address them with this request, kneeling with their right knee on the ground:
'O bhūtas dwelling among the devas of Mount Sumeru, those dwelling in the Nandana grove and other celestial palaces, those dwelling in...'"
They may dwell in the palaces of the sun and moon; or in rivers and seas; or in marshes, ponds, springs, and fountains;
or in villages and various shrines to deities; or in empty rooms; or in celestial mansions; or they may reside in monasteries and *caityas*;
or dwell in the grass huts of non-Buddhists; or in elephant stables; or in storehouses.
Some dwell in streets and alleys; some reside by the side of crossroads; some rely on solitary trees; some stay on great highways;
some live among burial mounds; some reside in śītavana charnel grounds; some take shelter in great forests;
some dwell in places where lions and tigers roam; some stay amidst vast sandy deserts; or some reside in various...
"O Exalted Ones who dwell in the most sublime places upon this continent, I beseech you all: together with your retinues, please descend to this place.
May you graciously partake of the flower garlands, ointments, incense, food, drink, and exquisite lamps that I have prepared;
may the fruits of the matters I seek be fully realized."
Having made offerings to the various spirits and ghosts, one should subsequently offer worship on a separate day to the deities who protect the directions.
Preparing the offerings as before, kneeling with palms joined, one should then invoke them:
"I respectfully invite the Deva Kauśika of the eastern direction, together with his retinue, to descend to this place of practice and graciously accept these offerings."
"Next, I invite the fire deities and celestial beings of the southeast, together with their retinues, to descend upon this ritual site; may you graciously accept these offerings.
Next, I invite Yama, the Dharma King of the south, together with his retinues, to descend upon this ritual site; may you graciously accept these offerings."
"Next, I invite the Great King Nīlabhūti and others from the southwest, together with their retinues, to descend upon this maṇḍala and graciously accept these offerings.
Next, I invite the Nāga King Varuṇa and others from the west, together with their retinues, to descend upon this maṇḍala and graciously accept these offerings."
"Next, I invite the Wind Deity King of the Northwest and his retinue to descend upon this ritual site; may you graciously accept these offerings.
Next, I invite Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, and his retinue to descend upon this ritual site; may you graciously accept these offerings."
"Next, I invite the Heavenly King Īśvara of the northeast, together with his retinue, to descend to this site of practice; may you graciously accept these offerings.
Next, I invite the Heavenly King Brahmā of the zenith, together with his retinue, to descend to this site of practice; may you graciously accept these offerings."

"Next, I invite all the great deity kings dwelling upon the earth, together with their retinues, to descend to this site of practice; each remaining in their respective directions, I pray that you accept the offerings prepared for you."
"Furthermore, may you always protect me.

By thus making offerings to the various spirits, ghosts, and deities who guard the directions, the practitioner will encounter no obstacles, and all that they seek and wish for will be completely fulfilled.
11. Chapter on the Differentiation of the Various Sections. *Subāhuparipṛcchā*, Chapter Eleven: "Furthermore, Subāhu, the youth!"
For the benefit of all sentient beings of the future, the World-Honored One has spoken three koṭis and five lakṣas of mantras and vidyās, which are called the Vidyādharapiṭaka.

Furthermore, the Noble Avalokiteśvara taught three koṭis and five lakṣas of mantras; within this family, the Lord of Mantras is named Hayagrīva (translated here as Mǎtóu), and the maṇḍala of this family is named Nivīya.
Furthermore, there are seven mantra-lords:

the twelve-armed one as a mantra-lord, the six-armed, the Ūrṇā-śikhin (Crown-tufted), the Pūrṇa-manoratha (Fulfiller of Wishes), the four-faced, the Amoghapāśa, and the two-armed. Just as the light of the sun illuminates the world, these seven mantra-lords are all governed by the Hayagrīva Maṇḍala.
"Furthermore, there are eight vidyārājñīs: Netrā, Śvetā, Śvetajaṭā, Lokanetrā, Ekajaṭā, Suvarṇavarṇā, Yaśovatī, and Bhṛkuṭī; these are all the vidyārājñīs within the Lotus Family."

Furthermore, I shall explain various wondrous maṇḍalas and mudrās; for the sake of benefiting impoverished sentient beings and subduing all classes of spirits, I shall teach seventy million mantras along with their maṇḍalas, as well as the ten messengers and the seven vidyārājñīs.

"Furthermore, there are sixty-four female attendants; there are eight great heart-mantras; there are immeasurable wrathful deities such as Kuṇḍalī; and there are immeasurable kings of mantras such as the most excellent vidyās."
"For this reason, this section is called the 'Extensive Vajra.
Furthermore, there is a great deity named Pañcika, who has spoken twenty thousand mantras."
This deity has a consort named Mikhara, who proclaims ten thousand mantras known as the Pañcika Section.
Furthermore, there is a great deity named Maṇibhadra, who proclaims one hundred thousand mantras;
the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa proclaims thirty thousand mantras, known as the Maṇi Section.

Furthermore, there were various devas and asuras who, before the World-Honored One, proclaimed immeasurable luminosities and various mantras. Among them, some entered the Vajra family, some entered the Lotus family, some entered the Pañcika family, some entered the Maṇi family, and some were not governed by any family. Regarding the aforementioned mantras, the various rules of practice have been briefly taught; one should practice all of them within the context of the five families.
"Furthermore, there are mantras spoken by various devas which have been authorized and permitted by the World-Honored One; these too should be practiced.
According to such rules, whoever rides upon this Dharma shall attain the fulfillment of their aspirations."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, within [the Buddha] there are also supreme and wondrous jewels; from these flow the ultimate jewels of the Dharma, from which in turn arise the eight kinds of great beings—the jewels of the non-retrogressive assembly. These Three Jewels are what the world extols."

Therefore, if a practitioner of recitation wishes to extinguish transgressions and generate merit, and hopes to swiftly attain the fulfillment of their present aspirations, they should first take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, if one wishes to maintain and recite mantras within the Vajra Family, after first taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one should next recite:
*Namaś-candavajrapāṇaye*.
"Mahāyakṣa Kṣetrapāte," and thereafter one should recite the mantra.
It is the same within the Lotus Family (Padmakula), the same in the Bhañjikā Family (Bhadrakulika), and for the Jewel Family (Maṇikula) as well, according to the aforementioned method.
First take refuge in the Triple Gem, next take refuge in the Lord of the Family, and only then may you recite the mantra.

If one does not take refuge in the teachings of the Śākya, or if one practices the Vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; if one’s faith is incomplete, harboring internal decay while outwardly displaying diligence, and further harbors stinginess and greed—one should not grasp this vajra of mine.
"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who disparage the profound and sublime Mahāyāna, saying that 'what is taught here is all the teaching of Māra.'"

Furthermore, harboring ignorance, they shall claim that the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva is a great yakṣa; they will fail to pay respect to the great bodhisattvas, giving rise to a mind of contempt, and for the sake of profit, they will falsely interpret [the teachings]. Such foolish people who maintain and recite these sublime mantras will, before long, bring harm upon their own lives.

As previously stated, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never intentionally harm others; however, within their retinues, there are various fierce and poisonous spirits who, upon seeing those foolish people who falsely grasp the vajra-pestle, give rise to wrath and immediately take their lives.
“Maheśvara-deva spoke ten koṭis of mantras;
Nārāyaṇa-deva-king spoke thirty thousand mantras;
Mahābrahmā-deva-king spoke sixty thousand mantras.”
"The Sun Deity spoke three hundred thousand mantras;
the King of Garuḍas spoke eighty-one thousand mantras;
and the Great Queen of Maheśvara spoke eight thousand mantras."
“The Fire King Deity spoke seven hundred mantras;
the Heavenly King Mātanga spoke three thousand mantras;
and the Queens of the Nāgas spoke five thousand mantras.”
The Great General of the Rākṣasas recited ten thousand mantras;
the Four Great Heavenly Kings recited four hundred thousand mantras;
and the Asura King recited two hundred thousand mantras.
"The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven spoke three hundred thousand mantras.
Each one also spoke their respective mantras, mudrās, and maṇḍalas; these should be received and maintained according to the dharma."
If one were to act according to this teaching without sincerity or truthfulness, it would likewise bring about self-destruction.
Chapter Twelve: The Section on the Analysis of the Eight Dharmas, Requested by the Youth Subāhu. "Furthermore, Youth Subāhu! [The Blessed One said:]..."
There are, in total, eight methods for accomplishment for those who practice recitation.
What are these eight? They are:

the method for accomplishing mantra, the method for accomplishing gold and water, the method for accomplishing longevity, the method for extracting hidden treasures, the method for entering the palace of the asuras, the method for synthesizing gold, the method for turning earth into gold, and the method for accomplishing priceless jewels. These are called the eight methods.
Within this, there are three [categories]:

the method for accomplishing mantra-dharmas, the method for entering the palaces of asuras, and the method for attaining longevity; these three types of methods are called the supreme-superior siddhi-dharmas.
The method for accomplishing priceless jewels, the method for turning earth into gold, and the method for revealing hidden treasures—these three types of methods are called the middling.
The method for compounding gold and the method for producing golden water—these two methods are termed the lower methods.
"If there are sentient beings who possess both ethical discipline and wisdom and delight in these methods, such persons shall delight in the supreme attainment."
"If there are sentient beings who have much craving for wealth and desire, such persons achieve middling accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings who, due to much ignorance, seek profit by overpricing their goods, such persons attain inferior accomplishment."
"Those of the highest caliber seek only the highest verification; they should not seek middling or lower evidence.
If one encounters those who are impoverished, one should seek the middling grade, neither seeking the highest verification nor taking the lowest evidence.
Those of the lowest caliber should seek according to the previous method, without alteration."
"If one wishes to attain the various accomplishments described above, one must cultivate merit.
A person endowed with merit who seeks the eight kinds of happiness previously mentioned—longevity, long life, power, sovereignty, physical beauty, and wisdom—shall achieve them all."

If a person, while still attached to their household affairs, cultivates wholesome dharmas, reverently keeps the Triple Gem in mind without ever departing from it, and recites mantras with constant mindfulness without interruption—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment; by keeping sentient beings in mind, they can further extinguish their own sins and obtain happiness in both this life and future lives.

Apart from mantras, there is no other method capable of bestowing happiness upon sentient beings. Just as when celestial fire descends or frost and hail fall, they can damage all things with no way to escape them; so too, the majestic power of mantras descends upon the mental fields of sentient beings, able to destroy suffering, affliction, and all karmic obstacles of sin, shattering them without remainder.

The sprouts of virtuous merit flourish day by day; like a wish-fulfilling jewel tree that can satisfy the various aspirations of sentient beings, so too is this wondrous treasury of mantras: it may grant the attainment of the stages and levels of a bodhisattva up to the fruit of Buddhahood, or the attainment of the stage of a vidyādhara, or the granting of wealth, happiness, physical vigor, and long life.

There are bodhisattvas who, observing sentient beings encountering various hardships and other fears—such as the calamities of kings, wicked bandits, fire, hail, and the like—immediately transform themselves into the form of a Mantra Lord to rescue and deliver those beings, enabling them to escape suffering and peril, and to dwell in peace, free from fear, with joy at their disposal throughout the full span of their lives.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, though living as a householder and enjoying various sensual pleasures, utters the Buddha’s mantras with the resolve to uphold them; yet, having attained but a small measure of the Dharma, they practice it only sporadically, their recitations are frequently accompanied by transgressions, and the ritual procedures they perform are largely incomplete.

That person does not take pleasure in daily recitation; whether the required number of repetitions has been reached or not, they stop midway. Their mind covets the mantras of other sections, yet those rites yield no efficacy. Consequently, they return to their former practice and focus their mind upon it; with the mind never ceasing its effort, the count shall gradually be fulfilled.

Suddenly perceiving some slight efficacy, his heart gave rise to joy; having rejoiced, he immediately confessed and revealed his transgressions, whereupon his offenses were extinguished. Freed from the obstacles of the five desires, he once again possessed the full substance of the precepts.

Having purified the body and entered a clean chamber, once one has further recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one must then perform the rite for seeking accomplishment (*sādhana*). Before long, one will attain the *siddhi* of the mantra as desired; thereafter, all other mantra rites that are performed will be successfully accomplished.
"Furthermore, Su-ba-hu youth!

When a practitioner of recitation is performing a ritual bath, they should take pure earth mixed with water and smear it all over their body. Then, entering the pure, great waters, they should wash as they wish. Having washed and facing either east or north, and having washed their hands and feet, they should place both hands within their knees, sprinkle water all over the body, and draw the water in silently, making no sound."

Immediately form the gesture of cupping water with the right hand, ensuring there are no bubbles within the palm. Recite the mantra over the water three times and inhale the water three times without making a sound. Wipe the mouth on both sides with the thumb and sprinkle water over the body, while uttering the protective sound.

Having completed the recitation for protection, one should then rinse with water as described above, drawn in through the mouth, whenever there is grime between the teeth, a sensation of contact on the tongue, or when coughing, sneezing, or spitting.

Having finished wiping the mouth and bathing, one should immediately proceed to a pure chamber; in the interim, one must not converse with or come into physical contact with any other outsiders—whether male or female, ordained or lay, pure Brahmins, boys, girls, or eunuchs.

If anyone has come into physical contact with you, first perform the ritual bathing, drinking water, and wiping the mouth as previously described; thereafter, do not speak with others, but enter a pure chamber to engage in recitation.
Even if urgent matters prevent you from resting, you must wait until the full number of days has elapsed before leaving the vihāra, and you must not accept offerings from others.
Having finished begging for food, you should perform your duties day and night without fail.
For such a person, the deities of the sublime mantras will enter their body with ease.

If one seeks accomplishment, while reciting the mantra, should there be a donor who offers clothing, gold, silver, precious gems, saddles and mounts, ornaments, unguents, incense, food and drink, bedding, or any such items—even down to a single hair’s breadth—one must not accept them.
"Furthermore, Su-ba-hu youth!

When a practitioner of recitation has finished urinating or defecating, they should use five portions of earth: three portions for washing after, one portion for washing before, and one portion for washing alone; thus they shall depart from the impure place and proceed to a pure place."

Divide the earth into ten portions. First, use three portions to wash the left hand alone; then, use seven portions to wash both hands. Afterward, take another three portions and thoroughly wash both hands, inside and out, until they are completely clean. Finally, use the remaining portion along with water to wash them thoroughly for ritual use.

For example, when the wind rubs against trees in the springtime, fire naturally emerges; with little effort, it burns through all the grass and wood. In the same way, using the fire of recitation and the wind of pure precepts to rub together with diligence, one likewise completely burns away the weeds of transgression.
Furthermore, just as frost is instantly dissolved by the sun's radiance, so too are the frosts of transgressions dissolved by the light of recitation, which functions like the sun of the precepts.

For example, if there has been darkness in a room for a long time, that darkness is immediately extinguished upon bringing a lamp inside; likewise, when the lamp of recitation illuminates the darkness of karmic obscurations, they are all completely eliminated.
By reciting the mantra up until the time of the homa offering, one shall attain accomplishment.

If this rite is not successful, one should take fine, pure sand from the ground near a river and fashion one hundred thousand stūpas with seals; these should be placed by the riverbank and the stūpas smeared with fragrant clay.

In this manner, before each and every stupa, one should recite the respective root mantra and perform the rite for the eradication of karmic hindrances through sincere repentance; thus, all sinful obstructions accumulated since beginningless time will be completely extinguished, and in this very life, one shall attain the fruition of manifest rewards.

"For those who perform recitation, the observance of the precepts is fundamental; they must be diligent and patient, harbor deep reverence for all Buddhas, resolve to attain Bodhicitta without ever turning back, and must constantly recite without any indolence."

For example, just as a king who possesses seven qualities is able to govern his subjects and ensure his own peace and happiness, so too does a person who recites this mantra possess these seven qualities; they thereby extinguish all sins and attain accomplishment.

At the outset, one should perform the recitation according to the Dharma without omission or error; by means of the *hūṃ* and *maḥ*, the tutelary deity is pleased and immediately bestows the fruits of desired happiness.
"Furthermore, Suvāhu,
if a practitioner of recitation wishes to accomplish the rite of gathering and delighting beings, even extending as far as a hundred *yojanas*, is this all through the power of the yakṣī?"

If one seeks to accomplish this dharma for the sake of sensual desire and becomes a yakṣiṇī, even if siddhi is attained, she will merely become the wife of a yakṣa; she is like a woman who sells her beauty, who desires a man only for the sake of looking at his wealth.
The yakṣī wives are likewise; even if one dwells together with them for an entire kalpa, they never harbor kind intentions, but instead watch for one's faults to harm and devour them.

Because foolish people, out of craving for other forms, desire to practice this method, once it is accomplished, they not only incur the fault of committing such deviant conduct, but will also surely suffer harm themselves.

This ritual for practitioners of recitation may not be abolished by others; those whose karma corresponds to it may practice this rite as they see fit. However, those within the Buddha-dharma who have a sincere inclination toward the path must not perform this procedure.
That which is not beneficial is the way of fools;
it is taught as a provisional manifestation for beginners and is not the true path.
"Furthermore, Suvāhu, the youth!..."

There are various bodhisattvas, vajras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others, who, before the Buddha and amidst the assembly of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, each recite their own mantras, with the World-Honored One serving as my witness.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, the Tathāgata has fully authorized and compassionately empowered this.
I shall now proclaim the mantras, which are of three grades:

"Those who achieve the superior grade shall ascend into the sky and depart, enter the palaces of the asuras, transform their bodies at will, become husbands of yakṣiṇīs, attain longevity, accomplish the dharmas of illusion and transformation, and transform their own bodies into those of Guhyapada and others."
"Those who achieve the middling grade obtain base wealth up to sovereign power and prosperity; their every intention follows their will.
Those of the lower grade cause people to hate one another, yet they can also bring them under their control, drive them from their kingdoms, and even cause them to wither away."

Regarding the lowest of the low [rites]: to treat those possessed by ghosts, spirits, nāgas, or demons, or infants, one causes the person to become drowsy and fall into deep sleep. One causes them to clench their fists or open their hands wide, or to grasp, bind, or embrace [the object]. One may also dispatch someone to whisper into their ear, or employ the *āveśana* (possession) rite involving whipping to drive out the spirit, even to the point of inflicting injury.

Furthermore, one may have a multitude of people recite mantras together; or have the people stamp their feet upon the ground, causing the possessed person to faint and collapse to the earth. Then, placing them at a crossroads, one covers them with white cotton cloth and has passersby look upon them.

Furthermore, they cause another person to slowly pull a white cotton cloth from the feet; as the cloth is pulled up until it is exhausted, the [subject] returns to their original state of mind. They also treat rat venom, seal the mouths of people, summon various dragons, bind many people so they cannot move, treat those afflicted by poison, and are able to transfer poison, use poison to poison others, and transform poison into human eyes. They also treat those who have been poisoned in return and issue prohibitions against the poison spreading.

They dispatch venomous snakes so they do not harm people, manifest themselves as humans or as messengers, and display themselves as humans or dragons for musical performances. They cure those possessed by malevolent spirits. All such categories are merely external dharmas and must not be relied upon or practiced.
"Furthermore, there are eighty species of venomous serpents in total.
Among them, twenty move with their heads held high.
Of these, six types coil their bodies when at rest."
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds that, though they bite people, are without venom.
Within this number, there is another thirteen snakes; their venom lies in the external earth.
Although other [insects] sting people, their venom may sometimes be present and sometimes absent.
Furthermore, there are various species such as frogs, *pígōng* (crabs), lizards, spiders, and diverse poisonous snakes and insects.
Although such classifications are numerous, those whose activity consists of fierce poison do not exceed six types:
"First, there are insects whose urine is filthy; their venom is lethal upon contact with humans."
"Second, there is the venom of attachment to the human body; it possesses poison immediately.
Third, there is the venom of contact; when the insect crawls, it cannot be seen by humans, yet if it touches a human body, it immediately possesses poison."
"Fourth, their saliva, when it comes into contact with a person, immediately becomes poisonous.
Fifth is the poison of the eyes; when these insects look at a person with their eyes, they immediately become poisonous."
"Sixth is 'Biting Poison. When these insects attach themselves to a person, they immediately inflict poison.
One who maintains the mantra does not fear their poison.
These various insects are categorized into superior, middling, and inferior grades, which together constitute several types of poison."

Therefore, other celestial deities have said that these various insects may release fierce venom because they are intoxicated by poison, or because of great anger, or out of fear, or due to hunger, or out of resentment, or when the time of death has arrived.
"There are four kinds of venom from a bite:
first, injury; second, bloodied wounds; third, severe damage; and fourth, death.
How is one to know when a bite has been poisoned?"
Where there is a single tooth mark at the site of the bite and the venom is slight, it is called a "scratch.
What is the nature of the "blood-smeared" poison?
It consists of two tooth marks that cause blood to flow; this is termed "blood-smeared."
"The poison that causes extreme damage has three tooth marks that cause the flesh to be wounded;
it is named 'Extreme Damage.
What are the characteristics of the poison that brings about the end of life?"
Wherever it bites, there appear four tooth marks; it then coils around the body, which is called "the end of life.
As for this poison, even the mantras of non-Buddhists or the most wondrous medicines are powerless to cure it.
It is like being burned by a fierce fire or cut with a blade; the suffering caused by poison is likewise.
For one who upholds the mantra, that poison is immediately extinguished, just as a raging great fire is extinguished when sprinkled with rain.
The subduing of poisons by mantras is likewise so.

The wise person, having a profound understanding of the various types of mudrās, plays with all manner of poisons while reciting the mantra of great majesty; they possess not the slightest fear, just as a lion king enters a herd of cattle without a single glance of apprehension.
"Furthermore, Subāhu Kumāra!

People in the world are constantly afflicted by various kinds of demonic illnesses: whether by the demons of devas, or nāgas, or asuras, or gandharvas, or garuḍas, or kiṃnaras, or mahoragas, or yakṣas, or rākṣasas, or those possessed by vidyādharas, or pretas, or piśācas, or kuṃbhāṇḍas."

As for the various kinds of ghosts and spirits mentioned above, they seek to see [offerings] for the sake of receiving sacrifices; or for the sake of playing tricks; or for the sake of killing and harming; or for the sake of wandering through the world to seek many profits; or because they constantly devour flesh and blood; or because they lie in wait to seek out the faults of others; or because they are constantly angry; or because they bind and seize sentient beings; or because their afflictions are fiercely blazing; or because of hunger; or because they bind sentient beings to cause their minds to become distracted; or because they sing or dance; or because they are joyful or sorrowful; or because they harbor grief and distress; or because they sometimes speak incoherently.

Regarding the various aforementioned anomalous signs that cause people to feel strange, laugh, or suffer from illness and so forth, one should perform ritual treatments using the Vajrāṅkuśa, the Amṛtakuṇḍalī, or the mantra of Krodhavajra; thus, they shall be cured and relieved.

For those afflicted by the aforementioned ailments, there are furthermore the mantras of the Fire God, the Wind God, Maheśvara, Mahābrahmā, Śakra-devendra of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Nārāyaṇa-devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the Sun and Moon devas, the Yakṣa King, and the Garuḍa King.

"Those malevolent spirits who do not fear the mantras of the aforementioned other external deities will naturally disperse upon merely hearing the name of Vajrāṅkuśa, let alone when one performs the ritual."
If one employs mantras to treat those who do not recover, the wise person should first understand the nature and conduct of the possessing spirits as well as the methods for their treatment;

only then will they be free from fear. Because the mantras spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are empowered by the Tathāgata’s grace, the mantras of other external deities cannot destroy those aforementioned mantras.

Furthermore, those who wish to extinguish their transgressions should, in a secluded and quiet place, construct a *caitya* using fragrant mud, or else one made of sand near a river, and place within it the verse on the Dharmakāya of Dependent Origination.

Having heard this Dharma, the Brahmās, yakṣas, vidyādhara maharṣis, garuḍas, gandharvas, bhūtas, and other such beings paid homage with deep respect and, joining their palms simultaneously, spoke these words:
“How marvelous! O Venerable One, you have compassion for all sentient beings!”
How rare is such subtle and wondrous compassionate conduct!

At times we see the Venerable One holding a brilliantly blazing great *vajra*, or a sturdy iron pestle, or a fierce and sharp wheel of fire; at times we see him holding the *Amoghapāśa* noose, or a three-pronged great trident, or a large horizontal sword, or a bow and arrow, or a staff; at times we see his weapons to be extraordinary and terrifying, or his marks and signs to be upright and majestic and thus pleasing, or we see the Venerable One acting as a yakṣa general.

We take refuge in the Great Compassionate One; as we practice, may the devas, asuras, humans, non-humans, and others constantly protect and mind us with deep-seated reverence, practicing according to the teachings without daring to forget them.

If, within this world of Jambudvīpa and the four continents, there are members of the fourfold assembly (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās), as well as boys and girls, who hear this Dharma, they shall, in their present life, be freed from suffering and calamity.
If one can practice all mantras according to the Dharma and the teachings, in accordance with this instruction, there is no doubt that one will obtain the siddhi as a karmic reward!
Having heard this supreme teaching, how much more so would one not obtain the fruit if one practices in accordance with the teachings?
Because we, the eight classes of followers, constantly and eternally protect those who practice the Way, no evil Māras, Vināyakas, yakṣas, or their like shall find any opportunity against them.

If there are impoverished sentient beings who rely on this Dharma teaching to uphold the vidyā-mantras, they will in this present life be freed from the suffering of poverty; they will attain wealth, nobility, and mastery, be revered by others, and be protected and guarded by all spirits and deities through their secret power.

If you wish to further seek the supreme, transcendent liberation, the aforementioned methods have already been set forth; practice according to the teachings as you please, with diligent effort and without regression. Before long, you shall attain the *vidyādhara-siddhi*, shining upon the world like the rising sun, free from all obstacles and with a mind undisturbed—provided you do not lack sincerity and remain untiring day and night. We, along with our retinues, shall never leave your side, assisting you with our power until the ultimate success is achieved.
Then the Lord Vajrapāṇi addressed them, saying:

"You gods, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, since you are able to follow my words, protect the mantras and the Mahāyāna treasury, as well as all sentient beings, and assist those who cultivate the path;

so too did I in the past assume the bodies of gods and nāgas, and receive all manner of powerful forms. Within those bodies, by means of my majestic power, I have constantly protected the Buddha-dharma, and out of compassion for sentient beings, I have assisted the efforts of those who cultivate the path regarding the Saṅgha Jewel, the Mahāyāna treasury, and the mantra secret scriptures, so that evil persons might find no opportunity and so that kings and ministers might not give rise to anger."
From the time I was an ordinary being until now, when I attained the state of a Vajradhara, this vow has never faltered or been abandoned.
Now that I have obtained such a body of wrathful mastery as a Vajradhara, if I look to the left or right,
or if my two eyes blink while observing the ten directions, all the worlds and lands of the universe will tremble in six ways.

From the Peak of Existence above down to the limits of the waters below, all the palaces and retinues of Māra within that space lost their radiance, appearing like a mass of ink beside a conch shell. All the palaces were shattered and destroyed like fine dust;
the various classes of asuras scattered in flight, naturally perishing, including all the members of Māra’s household.
They fainted and fell to the ground; some had bodies as if scorched by fire,
some were withered and parched, some lay amidst excrement and urine, some had their bodies crushed by mountains, some lay within icy mountains, some lay among the Cakravāḍa mountains,
and some lay upon the peaks of Mount Sumeru, hanging upside down on the verge of falling.
Those who are terrified; those who lie amidst the waves of great rivers and are seized by fear;
those who lie at the bottom of the ocean where they do not see the light of the sun or moon; those who lie in the air and suffer the torment of being scorched by the sun;
those who are hungry and cold; those who endure poverty; those who undergo the suffering of hell; and those who undergo the state of a preta.
As for their bodies: some take on the bodies of animals; some take on the bodies of birds; some take on the bodies of venomous snakes;
some are born having lost their original physical forms; some have fire emerge from their own bodies to burn them as they suffer;
some have fire issue from both eyes to burn their own faces; and some have female organs grow upon their male bodies.
Those who discharge impure and foul-smelling secretions; those who, though born as women, develop male organs on their bodies yet feel no shame;
those from whose mouths excrement and urine emerge; those being devoured by fierce beasts; those suffering pain from being bitten by snakes;
those who, while eating rice, have fire issue from their mouths, burning their tongues and scorching their teeth; or those whose hands and feet...
Those who have fallen [into hell], or whose bodies are swollen and rotting, or those lying ill, or those whose breath is about to cease, or those who are dead;
those suffering from spears and javelins, or suffering from flaming wheels, or suffering from swords and halberds;
those being trampled by white elephants, or those being gored to death by water buffaloes.
Or those who have been killed by others.

You gods, humans, and various other beings should know that because these celestial Māras constantly obstruct those who practice the Way, I now manifest the supernatural power of the samādhi of looking slightly to the right and left; even so, the retinues of these Māras immediately undergo such suffering and affliction—how much more so when one enters the fire-samādhi and manifests the *vaiśāradya* (fierce) supernatural powers!

From the past until now, because I have constantly protected those who cultivate this path and uphold the mantras, as well as the Buddha-dharma and all sentient beings, I have attained such power that even Māra is terrified and cannot look me in the face; how much more so could any evil person in the world fail to be afraid?

If there are bhikṣus or lay bodhisattvas who can give rise to the mind of a great man, reverently honor the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, protect the Mahāyāna scriptures and the Secret Treasury, and practice the dhāraṇīs and mantras, they will be able to restrain kings, ministers, and all evil persons, ensuring that these do not find an opportunity to cause harm.

Those who disparage me with evil words shall obtain blessings and attain supernatural powers and majestic authority equal to my own; all the Māras will be terrified and experience suffering, no different from what was mentioned before, and they shall receive their retribution upon reaching my abode.

“You gods, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, non-humans, and others, now before me, you have made great vows as adornments; protect the minds of sentient beings and, together with them, protect the treasury of the Dharma, providing them with supportive strength.”
Because your wholesome mind is so profound and vast, excellent!
Excellent! Most excellent indeed!
"You, too, shall before long attain the body of a Vajradhara; you will achieve the unimpeded mastery of *vaiśāradya* and subdue Māra and his host of enemies, becoming equal to me.
Then the Lord Vajradhara addressed the youth Subāhu:
"You must cause this to circulate in the world so that it is not forgotten or lost."
Then the youth Subāhu said:
"As Your Honor has instructed, I shall circulate this teaching from one to another and shall not dare to forget it.

At that time, the great assembly rose as one; the youth Subāhu, the eight classes of gods and humans, the Great Brahmā King, and the fourfold assembly encircled him several times, prostrated themselves with heads to the ground in reverent homage, and each made a solemn vow:
"May I and all sentient beings hear this Dharma and, practicing according to its teachings, swiftly attain such a body of great majestic power and strength.
Having prostrated once more at the feet of the Lord Vajradhara, each mounted their respective seat, took their leave, and returned to their palaces, suddenly vanishing from sight.
The Subāhuparipṛcchā Sūtra, Scroll II, Part B.
